<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study decodes the winning platform strategies behind TikTok's rapid rise in the social media ecosystem, aiming to provide generalizable insights for companies in the platform economy. It explores how TikTok overcame the formidable network effects of dominant platforms like Meta and identifies the platform strategies that fueled its unprecedented growth. The research offers a strategic framework for businesses aiming to innovate and grow in the competitive platform economy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A multi-faceted research approach was employed, including: 1) literature review on TikTok’s platform strategies, 2) on-the-ground observations of TikTok usage and trends, and 3) a comprehensive analysis of TikTok's platform design and features, user interface, and content distribution algorithms. This approach combined theoretical knowledge with practical insights.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study identified six key platform strategies driving TikTok's success: 1) Create a fun and immersive user experience; 2) Build network effects by supporting creators; 3) Harness human psychology in AI algorithms; 4) Foster viral dissemination via social Interactions; 5) Transform its weaknesses into strengths in competition; and 6) Cultivate a super-app with continuous innovation. These strategies enabled TikTok to rapidly gain market share and challenge established social media giants.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides novel insights into the platform strategies that enabled TikTok's unprecedented growth in the social media landscape. By dissecting TikTok's winning platform strategies, it offers valuable lessons for businesses seeking to innovate and succeed in the platform economy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The TikTok miracle: cracking the code of TikTok’s platform strategy

<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>The rise of Industry 4.0 led to digitally-enabled evolutionary and radical changes in all branches of the retail industry, resulting in the emergence of the distinct term “Retail 4.0”. Within this paradigm, particular emphasis is placed on forming a balanced system of omnichannel sales and customer service, allowing reaching a synergistic effect in the face of constant changes, turbulence and uncertainty in the business environment. The main objective of this study is to offer and justify a practical strategy for optimal utilization of sales channels and customer service provision within the Retail 4.0 paradigm.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>The conceptual argument of the study is based on the review of the literature and illustrative case studies</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>The decision-making model proposed in this study provides a roadmap for retailers. It underscores the need for a data-driven approach, where decisions are informed by real-time analytics and customer insights. This model also advocates for a flexible yet structured approach to managing various sales channels, ensuring that each channel complements and enhances the other.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>The study offers and justifies an original five-stage process model for forming a balanced system of omnichannel sales and customer service.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Strategy for striking the omnichannel balance in Retail 4.0

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to examine how governance factors and environmental practices influence the economic-environmental efficiency of organizations, in both the short and long-term.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis covers 3,483 observations from Brazilian firms listed on B3 between 2015 and 2022. The System Generalized Method of Moments (GMM-SYS) was employed to address endogeneity concerns. As an instrumental variable, the sectoral average of female board participation was used, calculated through the Leave-One-Out Mean approach.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicate that gender diversity on boards exerts a positive effect, although only in the long run. Recycling activities are associated with persistent efficiency gains, whereas financial leverage negatively affects efficiency only in the short-term. ESG ratings, while initially correlated with higher efficiency, display a reverse effect over time. This pattern may suggest a misalignment between market signaling and actual environmental performance when robust governance mechanisms are absent.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>From a social perspective, the results highlight the need for harmonized criteria and independent auditing, as well as the understanding that gender diversity policies require strategic patience. From a managerial standpoint, effective governance should convert institutional pressures into lasting, material actions, ensuring that investments, including leveraged ones, create value aligned with the SDGs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study’s originality lies in providing strong empirical support for Agency Theory and Institutional Theory, showing that the effects of governance structures and environmental practices on economic-environmental efficiency are contingent on the time horizon and on the materiality of actions. These findings have direct implications for SDGs 5, 9, 12, and 13.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Female board representation: a long-term strategy for leadership in economic-environmental efficiency and SDG integration

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper introduces the PIVOTAL Framework and the PIVOTAL Infinity Marketing Canvas®, a next-generation strategic model designed to link organizational purpose with innovation, stakeholder value, and long-term relationship building. The aim is to provide leaders with a practical, integrative approach for navigating strategic complexity in a rapidly changing environment. It is particularly relevant in transformation and innovation contexts, multi-stakeholder environments and ecosystem settings where legitimacy, adoption and long-horizon value matter.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper is conceptual in nature. It synthesizes established perspectives from strategic management, purpose-driven leadership, stakeholder theory, dynamic capabilities, service-dominant logic and relationship marketing to highlight theoretical gaps in existing models. Based on this analysis, it develops a unified framework and visual canvas that support strategic alignment and managerial decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The PIVOTAL Framework reconceptualizes strategy as a continuous, purpose-driven cycle connecting seven elements: Purpose, Innovation, Value, Outreach, Transfer, Advocacy and Lifetime Value. The PIVOTAL Infinity Marketing Canvas® operationalizes this logic by integrating organizational perspectives (purpose, innovation and value creation) with stakeholder perspectives (problems, pains, gains, values, advocacy and Lifetime Value). Illustrative examples demonstrate how organizations can apply the framework to enhance strategic coherence, stakeholder engagement and sustainable value creation. The framework helps leadership teams diagnose common disconnects (e.g., strong purpose but weak transfer; high outreach but unclear value; innovation without advocacy) and align initiatives accordingly.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As a conceptual and practitioner-oriented paper, the PIVOTAL framework has not yet been empirically validated across contexts. This limitation offers clear avenues for research: future studies can test whether the Canvas improves strategic alignment, innovation focus, adoption (“transfer”), advocacy and long-term value outcomes using multi-case designs, executive surveys or longitudinal data. Comparative research could assess incremental usefulness versus established canvases and strategy tools, and identify boundary conditions (e.g., industry turbulence, regulation, ecosystem dependence, cultural context). Further work can refine measurement approaches for transfer, advocacy and lifetime value in purpose-led transformation initiatives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As a conceptual and practitioner-oriented article, the PIVOTAL framework has not yet been empirically tested across settings. Future research could examine how well the Canvas improves strategic alignment, innovation focus, adoption (“transfer”), advocacy and long-term value outcomes, using multi-case studies, executive surveys or longitudinal designs. Studies could also explore boundary conditions (e.g., industry turbulence, regulation, ecosystem dependence, cultural contexts) and compare PIVOTAL with established canvases to assess incremental usefulness. In addition, research could refine measurement approaches for transfer, advocacy and lifetime value in purpose-led transformation initiatives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework encourages organizations to move beyond short-term optimization by embedding purpose, stakeholder value and long-term relationships into strategic decision-making. By strengthening “transfer” from intent to adoption and fostering advocacy, PIVOTAL supports more responsible implementation, trust-building and transparency—especially in contexts where societal legitimacy matters. This can contribute to better stakeholder outcomes such as fairer value creation, more sustainable innovation choices and stronger customer and employee relationships. When applied thoughtfully, the approach can help organizations align growth objectives with broader social value and long-term resilience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper contributes a holistic strategic model that bridges theory and practice by positioning purpose as the central organizing principle of strategy. It extends existing frameworks by integrating innovation, stakeholder value, relational dynamics and long-term advocacy into a unified strategic logic. The Canvas offers leaders a practical, action-oriented tool for orchestrating strategy, collaboration and organizational alignment across functions. Unlike specialist tools that focus mainly on business model design or value propositions in isolation, PIVOTAL provides an end-to-end leadership architecture linking purpose to execution (“transfer”), advocacy and long-term value outcomes. It is designed to complement rather than replace established canvases by making the missing links between strategic intent and adoption explicit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Leading with purpose: the PIVOTAL Infinity Marketing Canvas for strategy, innovation and long-term value

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper investigates how participation of internal actors influences financial performance. We analyze how various combinations of strategic activities shape financial performance when involving respectively top management, middle management, and the whole workforce.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We develop a theoretical model using a combinatorial view of the strategy process and practices as entities to examine how specific strategic activities influence financial performance. We have completed a quantitative study with more than 2,100 respondents from private companies located in Denmark. We asked top managers, middle managers and employees about strategy work and financial performance of their companies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings show that combining top management, middle management and workforce participation driven approaches to strategy work have a positive effect on financial performance. The effect grows the more the internal strategy actors participate – just a little when middle managers participate but a lot when also the employees participate in the strategy work. Participation is embedded within the three strategy activities: (1) communicating the strategy across all organizational levels, (2) translating the strategy into action plans at each level, and (3) allocating resources in alignment with strategic priorities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study goes beyond the traditional strategy entity or process approach, and uses a combinatory approach of process and practice on strategy work combined with an entity approach. Normally, questionnaires are distributed to top managers when investigating strategy. We included middle managers and employees as respondents, meaning that the questionnaire encompasses all types of actors (strategy champions) that can be part of or influence the strategic work of the organization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Strategy work: the impact of participation from top management, middle management, or workforce on financial performance

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For decades, a significant number of studies have examined the agenda of the formalization of artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) operations. There is now enough anecdotal evidence that formalization of ASM operations can help promote safe working conditions. However, very few studies have examined the internal dynamics and outcomes once ASM operations become formalized. This notwithstanding, these few studies provide very useful insights that could help reshape policy and refine scholarly ideas about formalization. This present study, therefore, performs the task of (re)visiting the empirically oriented insights of the literature that explores the ASM activities of operators that are in possession of mining licenses and are in operation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study seeks to answer the following question: How far have formalization mechanisms succeeded in “sanitizing” the ASM sector? To achieve this, the authors draw on the findings of qualitative case studies examining the operations of formal ASM actors. Other data for the inquiry were sourced from published documents providing insights and discussions on the dynamics of the formalization of ASM.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Synthesizing the findings of the studies that have examined formalized ASM operations, the evidence seems to suggest that monitoring and supervision can mediate good environmental management practices. Formalization seems to have positive impacts on the working conditions and the health and safety of the operators; however, this might not be true for access to credit, reinforcing the fact that unaided formalization cannot completely cure the excesses of informality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Analyzing the literature on formal ASM operations, this present study provides useful discussions of where we stand and how research and policy discussions on ASM formalization may proceed from here.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Formalization as a strategy of ASM “sanitization”: So far, how far?

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates how Hybrid Strategy and Sustainability Orientation jointly influence SME performance, emphasizing the mediating roles of Product, Process, and Social Innovation across financial, market, and social dimensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on the Resource-Based View, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, and Stakeholder Theory, the study develops and tests a conceptual framework using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling. Data were obtained from a cross-sectional survey of SMEs in emerging markets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Both Hybrid Strategy and Sustainability Orientation significantly enhance all three forms of innovation. Product innovation emerged as the most influential, particularly in driving financial and social performance. Process innovation contributed strongly to market performance. Social innovation showed meaningful effects on social outcomes but was not significantly linked to financial performance, indicating varied contributions of innovation types across performance dimensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings provide actionable insights for SME managers and policymakers. Integrating cost-efficiency with differentiation and sustainability orientation boosts innovation outcomes. Managers should prioritize product and process innovation for immediate gains while pursuing social innovation as a long-term strategy to build stakeholder trust. Policymakers are encouraged to support these dual strategies through targeted innovation programs and incentives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study develops a novel integrative framework that links two strategic orientations Hybrid Strategy and Sustainability Orientation with multidimensional SME performance (financial, market, and social) through the distinct mediating roles of product, process, and social innovation. It is among the first to empirically disentangle these innovation pathways within resource-constrained and sustainability-driven contexts, offering a more nuanced and evidence-based understanding of strategic innovation in SMEs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Hybrid strategy, sustainability orientation, and SME performance: the mediating role of product, process, and social innovation

                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this study is to develop a formative framework of brand communities as an alternative strategy to guide marketing and public relations professionals in managing consumer relationships. In doing so, the study explores the motivations that drive brand community membership, the ritualistic practices that create community engagements, and the specific benefits brands derive from their represented brand communities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study adopts a qualitative approach, predicated on focus group discussions and semi-structured interviews. This approach enabled an in-depth exploration of participants’ motivations, practices, and lived experiences relating to brand community participation and management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study identifies six key motivations driving brand community membership, with access to hidden tips and updates, reducing consumer loneliness, and psychological ownership emerging as central drivers. The findings further reveal distinct ritualistic practices, including the use of symbolic gestures, member initiation rites, and philanthropic activities that reinforce a sense of belonging and engagement within the brand communities. From the brand managers’ perspective, we observed that brand communities generate strategic benefits such as real-time consumer insights and feedback, heightened commitment and oppositional loyalty, positive brand evangelism, support for issues and crisis management, and reduced promotional costs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to brand community scholarship by moving beyond dominant outcome-oriented themes to develop a formative framework. Based on the empirical findings, the study proposes a strategic framework centered on the Formation, Engagement, and Benefits of brand communities, offering both theoretical insights and practical guidance for marketing and public relations professionals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Developing a formative framework of brand communities as an alternative strategy for marketing and public relations practitioners in emerging markets

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Environmental challenges such as climate change and resource scarcity have placed considerable pressure on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to embrace sustainable practices. This study examines the impact of Environmental Sustainability Orientation (ESO), Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), and Green Transformational Leadership (GTL) on firm performance (FP) through Green Innovation (GI) in SMEs of United Arab Emirates (UAE).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis is based on 424 observations and employs Partial Least Squares–Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to explore the interrelationships among the examined constructs, thereby providing insights into their combined effects on firm performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results reveal that CSR robustly fosters green innovation and subsequently improves firm performance. Moreover, GTL exerts both a direct influence on performance and an indirect influence via innovation. ESO predominantly contributes to promoting green innovation and boosting firm performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By integrating Natural Resource-Based View (NRBV) and Stakeholder Theory, the study underscores how sustainable practices can provide a competitive advantage. It offers practical insights for SME leaders, stressing the importance of embedding sustainability into core strategies to drive long-term performance and competitiveness in dynamic markets like the UAE.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Sustainability as strategy: how environmental sustainability orientation, CSR and green leadership drive firm performance via innovation in SMEs

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper provides a comprehensive examination of transactional, transformational, and servant leadership theories, evaluating their relevance across contemporary organizational sectors. It also explores how emerging paradigms, like hybrid, inclusive, authentic, and agile leadership build upon classical frameworks to meet evolving challenges.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper applies a theory-based conceptual analysis, supplemented with real-world illustrations and sector-specific examples. The research includes a comparative evaluation of leadership styles, integrating insights from academic literature and applied organizational practices. The focus is placed on connecting leadership behaviors with contextual demands and emerging trends.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis finds that while each leadership theory offers distinct advantages, their effectiveness depends on situational and sectoral factors. Leaders often benefit from adopting a flexible, integrative approach that blends elements of all three styles. The study also highlights how new leadership models such as agile and inclusive leadership build upon traditional theories to meet modern workplace challenges.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This conceptual analysis may be complemented by future empirical studies to validate findings across specific industries and cultural settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Leaders and HR professionals can use the findings to tailor their leadership development strategies and adapt to sector-specific leadership demands.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study adds value by combining foundational leadership theories with current applications and emerging trends. It broadens the scope of existing literature by linking classical leadership frameworks with practical implications for evolving organizational environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Exploring leadership theories: a comprehensive analysis

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Finding meaning, both in life and at work, is increasingly difficult. Work innovations like AI, robotics, and remote work only intensify this challenge, leaving growing numbers of workers feeling disconnected and unfulfilled. Effective work and meaningful experience don’t need to be at odds. In fact, the most successful organizations regularly prove the opposite to be true. This article makes the case that meaningful work is not a cultural amenity or a management fashion, but rather, it is a powerful precondition for sustainable organizational success, that can be attained through careful design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on research from a forthcoming book on the role of intrinsic needs in living meaningfully, the article models how six primary human needs – Utility, Belonging, Learning, Spirituality, Altruism, and Autonomy – can be applied to design meaningful, high-performing workplaces. The Six Senses framework is mapped against four decades of organizational excellence research, from Peters and Waterman, to Jim Collins and Toyota’s Production System.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article defines of each of the six intrinsic needs, and brings related concepts, tools and methods to life through rich organizational examples and an in-depth application to a single case of a high-performing research firm.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By placing meaningfulness at the center of organizational design, and foregrounding six intrinsic human needs, the article opens a world of novel possibilities that is both relatable and practically achievable. Its treatment of AI, robotics, and remote work through this lens offers a powerful and nonobvious way to address one of the most pressing challenges facing organizations and workers today.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The meaningful enterprise: building organizations fit for humans

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to investigate the role of transformational leadership in the sustainable performance of local public administration by examining how transformational leaders influence the achievement of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) objectives within Portuguese local government entities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The sample includes a panel of 211 respondents who work in government entities in Portugal through the application of structural equation modelling (SEM). This approach enables the simultaneous examination of both the direct effects of transformational leadership on sustainable performance and the indirect effects mediated by corporate social responsibility and organizational politics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results demonstrate that transformational leadership positively influences both corporate social responsibility (CSR) and sustainable performance, but the hypothesized indirect/mediating effect of CSR was not statistically supported. Conversely, organizational politics neither significantly affects sustainable performance nor mediates the relationship between transformational leadership and sustainable performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The empirical insights provided by this study offer important insights for public managers and policymakers interested in promoting sustainable governance practices in local governments Beyond their practical implications, the results offer an original contribution to the public administration literature by extending transformational leadership research to the context of local government, an institutional setting that has received comparatively limited empirical attention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Transformational leadership and sustainable performance of local government

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines the velocity trap in which organizations optimize execution speed while strategic relevance deteriorates, and introduces the Strategic Event Horizon and Velocity Gambit as a structured rescue maneuver for senior leaders.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Conceptual, practice-grounded article drawing on the Standish Group’s CHAOS Report (n = 50,000 projects), dual practitioner surveys (n = 105), and case study (n = 25, 12 interviews), interpreted through Red Queen competition theory, Boyd’s OODA Loop, and Lean Startup literature.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 36-percentage-point gap separates projects hitting targets (57%) from those achieving strategic goals (21%), illustrating systematic velocity-value decoupling. The supporting case material surfaces the work vs improvement dichotomy as a recurring constraint, while the Velocity Gambit organizes Boyd’s OODA Loop into a four-phase managerial decision protocol. An illustrative cloud-native platform case shows how the protocol can be applied in practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The evidence base is illustrative rather than confirmatory: the case evidence is single-site, the surveys are convenience-sampled, and the CHAOS data remains proprietary. Future work should test the framework across industries and with longitudinal designs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides diagnostic indicators for velocity-value decoupling, a four-phase OODA-mapped intervention, organizational readiness prerequisites, and governance guardrails. The velocity trap extends beyond financial costs to burnout and talent attrition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study formalizes the Strategic Event Horizon, operationalizes Boyd’s OODA Loop for established firms, and bridges Red Queen theory with Lean Startup pivot protocols, providing decision architecture where psychological substrates prevent incremental self-correction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The velocity gambit: agile in the strategic event horizon

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper examines how CEOs and managing directors lead AI transformation and how their leadership approaches shape organizational change.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study draws on 31 qualitative interviews with CEOs and managing directors across diverse industries in Finland. Inductive thematic analysis is used to identify and compare distinct leadership approaches to AI transformation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three approaches are identified: Generalist, Expert, and Disruptive. Generalists delegate AI execution to specialists while maintaining strategic alignment and resource support. Experts lead hands-on, building AI capabilities and embedding AI into strategy and management practices. Disruptors treat AI as an existential shift and pursue bold moves, including business-model and market repositioning. The approaches differ in engagement level, scope of change, and typical risks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper extends upper echelons and transformational leadership research by showing how CEOs’ personal orientation to AI shapes AI transformation outcomes, and it offers a practical framework for aligning leadership approach with AI maturity and strategic intent.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Leading AI transformation: three approaches for CEOs

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Research on organizational change capability (OCC) is a relatively novel and rapidly growing field of study. Recent advances show that definitions of the concept of organizational change capability are scarce. Furthermore, empirical studies defining the concept of organizational change capability appear absent. This paper addresses these shortcomings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper approaches the concept of OCC both via a literature review, and empirically via a multiple case study, mapping how organizations’ change-makers (executive board members, directors, managers and specialists) view the concept of OCC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper distinguishes between two neighboring concepts, organizational change capability (OCC) and organizational change capacity. A typology is suggested, where extant definitions of OCC can be categorized into evolving or fixed perspectives. Furthermore, this paper’s multiple case study findings suggest approaching organizational change capability via four clusters of capabilities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>From a practitioner perspective, the results of this paper provide organizations with much-needed guidance for better assessing and developing their capabilities in change. Organizations and practitioners may now approach organizational change capability via the empirically grounded model of organizational change capability, suggested in this paper.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To the best of the author’s knowledge, this is the first study to approach the concept of OCC through an empirical lens. An empirically grounded model of organizational change capability is suggested, comprising four clusters of capabilities: skilled resources and a culture supporting individuals in change; a functioning framework; change-enabling processes and coordination; and two-way systems. Finally, a novel definition of OCC is suggested.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Organizational change capability: toward a conceptual and empirical definition

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this paper is to challenge the implicit assumption in the resource-based view (RBV) that effective value creation requires continuous, and comprehensive reconfiguration of a firm’s entire resource portfolio.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A conceptual approach by integrating the RBV with institutional theory. A mechanism-based framework is developed to explain how managerial selectivity in resource orchestration shapes value realization under conditions of institutional embeddedness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper introduces selective resource orchestration as a managerial capability of selective discrimination between resources that require adaptation and those that should be preserved. The framework demonstrates how selective orchestration sustains valuable, rare, inimitable and non-substitutable (VRIN) attributes by structuring managerial attention and temporally decoupling institutional adaptation from core resource stability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study extends the RBV by reconceptualizing resource orchestration as a selective, rather than comprehensive, managerial process. It theorizes intentional restraint as a core mechanism for preserving causal ambiguity and path dependence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework provides guidance for managers operating in institutionally embedded contexts by clarifying when restraint – rather than continuous adaptation – enhances value realization while maintaining the foundations of competitive advantage.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper offers a novel extension of the RBV by introducing selective resource orchestration and specifying the mechanisms and boundary conditions under which managerial restraint contributes to value creation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Selective resource orchestration: rethinking how firms realize value

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper explores the use of agile responses in organizations at three different management levels: CEO, executive team and enterprise wide. The authors compare and contrast three different case examples to highlight that each organizational level involves different goals, processes, skill sets, challenges and solutions. These cases underscore the need to define agility more precisely across different levels, business functions and contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The authors examined the growing literature on strategic agility and developed a bespoke agility survey via an executive program with supply chain managers in Asia, as fully shown in the Appendix. The survey itself, plus the pilot data that the authors collected and summarized, underscore the need to customize survey-based agility measures to specific organizational or functional settings. The authors’ three main business cases illustrate this further at different levels in an enterprise.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The authors’ analysis shows that strategic agility can differ greatly from operational agility and that each type can vary markedly across situations and organizational levels. The lack of clear definitions of agility in the academic literature complicates attempts at general taxonomies or prescriptive guidance that is invariant across cases.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The three cases the authors selected for comparison and contrast were based on their own familiarity with the respective situations. Each was also widely covered in general business news when the authors wrote this paper. In the absence of an agreed taxonomy for business situations involving agility, these practice-based cases helped to illustrate the conceptual points the authors wanted to make.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The best remedy in practice would be for leaders to examine how agility is currently defined in their own organization across level and functions, by means of surveys, interviews or external benchmarks. With that in hand, agility alignments can be better tailored and improved.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper contributes to the agility literature by highlighting its weak conceptual foundations in theory and by highlighting the contextual nature of agility in practice. By separating agility into CEO, executive-team and enterprise-wide levels, the authors offer a framework for resolving the concept’s persistent definitional ambiguity. This multi-level perspective also helps practitioners clarify which type of agility they are trying to deploy. It also helps avoid one-size-fits-all prescriptions and improve the practical value of agility oriented initiatives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Strategic leadership and agility in organizations

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This integrative review synthesizes research on adaptive, agile, complexity and ambidextrous leadership and innovation under VUCA (volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity) to clarify how leaders orchestrate context-sensitive (“contingent”) innovation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Guided by Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020, we searched Scopus (December 29, 2025), screened 85 records and synthesized 34 journal articles (2015–2025). We appraised evidence [Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT)-informed for empirical papers; conceptual-rigor checklist for conceptual papers] and analyzed it using a concept-centric coding matrix.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four themes recur: (1) leadership as sensemaking/framing and enabling experimentation; (2) innovation as exploration–exploitation balancing (ambidexterity), often expressed at the level of an evolving innovation initiative portfolio; (3) psychological safety, trust, organizational support and self-efficacy as mechanisms for innovative work behavior; and (4) dynamic capabilities that transform experiments into reconfiguration. We develop a four-proposition framework that integrates these themes by specifying mediation pathways and boundary conditions (portfolio governance routines and coordination overload).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Theory-building synthesis; propositions require empirical testing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework serves as a diagnostic and action tool and provides scenario-based leadership routines for balancing experimentation with disciplined alignment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We define contingent innovation capability as an organizational orchestration capability–comprising sensing, portfolio governance and integration/reconfiguration routines–and explain how adaptive leadership behaviors develop and activate it to couple safe-to-fail experimentation with disciplined integration as contingencies shift.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Leading through complexity: an integrative review and contingent innovation framework

<jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This conceptual paper investigates the phenomenon of “leader-turn-follower,” which refers to individuals previously in leadership roles transitioning into follower positions due to changes such as political shifts or evolving skill demands. The focus is on understanding how a leader-turn-follower demonstrates commitment to achieving organizational goals under a new leader by leveraging their experience, or if they might undermine the new leader, driven by resentment or a sense of loss of authority.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The paper sheds light on the construct of leader-turn-follower. It sets the stage for future research to explore the factors influencing whether these individuals support or sabotage new leadership.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The study identifies an important question that remained unanswered in previous studies and needs further study. It highlights the need to examine the conditions under which a leader-turned-follower will support or sabotage the new leader’s efforts to achieve organizational goals. It identifies the potential for positive contributions, where leader-turn-followers use their insights and expertise to enhance the new leader’s effectiveness, and negative behaviors, where they may engage in sabotage.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As a conceptual paper, the study’s propositions are theoretical and require empirical validation through future research.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The study assists organizations in implementing measures that foster collaboration and mitigate the risk of sabotage by the leader-turned-follower.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper introduces the concept of leader-turn-followers to leadership studies, an area previously neglected. It offers new insights into the dynamics of organizational commitment and the potential conflicts or collaborations that arise when leaders become followers.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
title: Leader-turn-follower: an opportunity for cooperation or sabotage?

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines the relationship between corporate social responsibility (CSR) performance and financial performance, focusing on the moderating role of managerial entrenchment. The research aims to understand how entrenched managers influence the effectiveness of CSR initiatives and their impact on financial outcomes, particularly in the context of stringent French regulations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study employs a generalized least squares (GLS) econometric model to analyze a panel of 120 companies listed on the SBF 120 index from 2011–2022. The model integrates Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) scores, managerial entrenchment indicators and financial data to isolate the effects of CSR and governance on performance. Managerial entrenchment is measured using a novel composite index combining CEO tenure, CEO-Chairman duality and anti-takeover provisions. Robustness tests, including alternative measures and sectoral subsampling, are conducted to ensure the reliability of the results.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results reveal a significant positive relationship between CSR performance and financial performance, supporting stakeholder theory. However, managerial entrenchment negatively moderates this relationship, as entrenched managers tend to prioritize superficial, media-friendly CSR initiatives over substantive, long-term investments. This strategic misalignment reduces the financial benefits of CSR, particularly in firms with high levels of managerial entrenchment. Additionally, robust governance mechanisms, such as board independence and size, positively influence financial performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study is limited by its focus on French firms listed on the SBF 120, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings to other contexts. Future research could explore cultural and sectoral variations, as well as the impact of crises (e.g., pandemics, energy transitions) on CSR strategies. The study also calls for further investigation into the underlying mechanisms of managerial entrenchment and its interaction with CSR innovation and reputation</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings suggest that companies should adopt a balanced approach to CSR and governance. Implementing term limits for CEOs, creating independent CSR committees and integrating measurable ESG indicators into executive compensation can help align managerial incentives with stakeholder interests. Firms should also invest in green technologies and sustainable business models to mitigate the negative effects of managerial entrenchment on CSR effectiveness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study highlights the importance of ethical governance in ensuring that CSR initiatives serve the common good rather than personal legitimization. By promoting transparency and accountability, companies can build trust with stakeholders and contribute to sustainable development. The research underscores the need for regulatory reforms to strengthen corporate governance and align CSR strategies with societal expectations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research makes a significant contribution to the business ethics literature by empirically validating the positive impact of corporate social responsibility (CSR) on financial performance, while simultaneously exposing the ethical myopia associated with managerial entrenchment. Its originality stems from a triple contribution that addresses key gaps in the field. First, it offers an important contextual advancement by focusing on France’s distinct stakeholder-oriented model, providing a crucial counterpoint to the dominant body of research centered on Anglo-Saxon market-based systems. Second, it delivers a methodological innovation through the creation of a novel, multi-dimensional entrenchment index that captures the complexity of this phenomenon beyond traditional proxy measures. Finally, and most substantially, it provides a theoretical breakthrough by revealing entrenchment’s dual role as both a driver of organizational stability and a negative moderator of CSR efficacy. This crucial finding helps reconcile conflicting perspectives in the literature by demonstrating how the same governance mechanism can simultaneously support certain organizational objectives while undermining ethical performance, thereby offering a more nuanced understanding of the complex relationship between governance structures, ethical decision-making and financial outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: CSR vs entrenchment: the silent battle impacting French business outcomes

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study − theoretically and empirically − advances a concept of coherence to explain the internal structure responsible for a firm’s structural ambidexterity. Coherence appeals to an orthogonal view that exploitation and exploration are not conflicting learning processes, but instead are mutually related. This coherence offers a network structure in which strong and weak ties are related in complementary ways. These complementarities enable a firm’s coherence to jointly leverage the exploitive and explorative properties of these strong and weak tie networks and thus offer an orthogonal explanation of a firm’s structural separation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By drawing on Teece’s (1994) corporate concept of coherence and Granovetter’s (1973, 1983) strength of tie arguments, the orgothonal properties of coherence are examined. In addition, as coherence emphasizes the differentiation or specialization of a firm’s experiences, a firm’s diversity of knowledge expertise offer benefits of structural ambidexterity. Hypotheses were developed to examine the performance implications of this structural ambidexterity arguments. In using an Arellano-Bond (1991) and Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS) estimation approach, panel estimations of the U.S. biotechnology industry were used to examine these hypotheses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study’s panel estimations find that coherence and diversity have a positive and negative moderating influence on a firm’s performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study’s concept of coherence offers a balance where exploitation and exploration mutually reinforces a firm’s ability to adapt to dynamic markets. This offers an 'orchestration of skills’ that advances a firm’s higher order dynamic capabilities. As a result, coherence not only advances dynamic capabilities research, but it also addresses calls for more dynamic explanations of the structural ambidexterity concept.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study suggests that when managers institute their firm’s diversity policies, the social demands for diversity may need to be weighed against the integration benefits of a firm’s coherence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A key contribution of this study is that coherence offers an orthogonal view that resolves the conflicts in a firm’s exploitation and exploration and thus offering an important source of structural ambidexterity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Having it both ways: a coherence view of structural ambidexterity

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mid-level educational leaders in universities are responsible for educational quality yet lack formal managerial authority. This study examines how they exercise compassionate leadership while re-sponding to competing organisational responsibilities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study draws on semi-structured interviews with 15 mid-level educational leaders across facul-ties at a large Danish university. Using an abductive approach, it brings Max Scheler’s phenomeno-logical account of compassion into dialogue with the empirical material to explore compassionate leadership among mid-level educational leaders.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants described responsibility as requiring attention and action when colleagues struggle, stu-dents are affected or problems arise in educational practice. They described attending to colleagues’ and students’ concerns while also responding to organisational responsibilities. Their accounts in-cluded explaining decisions, providing reassurance, coordinating activities, representing concerns within the organisation and addressing conditions that affect others. At the same time, recognising others’ difficulties does not in itself determine what should be done. Rather, leaders remained re-sponsive to others while carrying out their educational and organisational responsibilities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study suggests that compassionate leadership involves remaining responsive to colleagues’ and students’ concerns even when institutional responsibilities require actions that do not alleviate those concerns. It extends existing accounts of compassionate leadership by drawing on Scheler’s phenomenology of compassion, which has received little attention in leadership research. Rather than understanding compassion as a sequential process of recognising suffering and acting to alleviate it, the analysis conceptualises compassion as fellow-feeling: a distinct act that may accompany, but does not determine acts of leadership. This distinction makes it possible to understand leadership situations as encompassing compassion alongside judgement and responsibility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Compassionate mid-level educational leadership in higher education

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper aims to explore how empathetic leadership can serve as a humanizing force in artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated workplaces, where algorithmic decision-making increasingly shapes performance evaluation, communication and workflow design. It reframes empathy not as a soft interpersonal trait but as a strategic leadership capability needed to balance data-driven logic with emotional and ethical judgment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This is a conceptual paper that integrates theories of emotional intelligence, servant leadership and sociotechnical systems through an interpretive theoretical synthesis to develop a framework for empathetic leadership in algorithmic work settings. The framework is anchored in organizational justice theory; specifically, the procedural, distributive, interactional and informational justice dimensions to explain how empathetic leadership compensates for the justice deficits that algorithmic systems produce. A critical perspective on empathy’s limits, including performative risks and potential for moral outsourcing, is also integrated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper argues that empathetic leadership becomes most valuable when leaders act as translators between algorithmic feedback and human experience. Three leadership functions emerge as critical: (1) interpreting data without dehumanizing people, (2) protecting psychological safety when automation increases uncertainty, and (3) mitigating bias and inequity embedded in AI systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study offers a conceptual contribution rather than empirical validation, and therefore its claims require future investigation through qualitative and mixed-method approaches in organizational settings. The focus on AI-mediated decisions also limits generalizability to contexts where automation is minimal.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Leaders will need new capabilities for emotional sensemaking in data-intensive environments, including mindful listening, ethical questioning of algorithmic outputs, and intentional relationship-building in digitally mediated workflows. Organizations must redesign leadership development to incorporate empathy as an evidence-based skill, not an intuitive behavior.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As AI systems influence hiring, promotion, performance scoring and task automation, leaders hold moral responsibility for preserving dignity, fairness and trust. Empathetic leadership can counteract the depersonalization risks of algorithmic control and support more inclusive, human-centered workplaces.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper contributes a conceptual framework that positions empathy as a structural governance capability, anchored in organizational justice theory and explicitly differentiated from existing leadership models through theoretical comparison. The central argument is that existing models assume human-to-human relational fields, whereas the Empathetic Algorithmic Leadership Framework is designed for the human-to-algorithm-to-human relational field created by algorithmic management. It extends leadership literature by integrating AI ethics, emotional intelligence and organizational design into a single model of “empathetic-algorithmic leadership.”</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Empathetic leadership in the age of AI: humanizing the algorithmic workplace

<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>Beyond its initial hype, and based on original new surveying, this paper explores the impact of metaverse on business in the medium to long-term.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Methodology</jats:title>
<jats:p>IBM Institute for Business Value, in collaboration with Oxford Economics, surveyed 400 C-Suite executives, (CEOs, CIO/CTOs and CMOs) in the U.S. across 25 industries on their investments in metaverse, business cases and outcomes.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:list list-type="bullet" id="list1">
<jats:list-item><jats:p>Despite the media hype, the majority of investment in metaverse is B2B.</jats:p></jats:list-item>
<jats:list-item><jats:p>Although the biggest impacts of metaverse are medium to long-term, there are benefits immediately accessible in the short-term.</jats:p></jats:list-item>
<jats:list-item><jats:p>More success is likely if organizations develop metaverse strategies with ecosystem partners.</jats:p></jats:list-item>
</jats:list>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Research implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>Metaverse was extremely fashionable, now far less so. Both extremes are inappropriate. Metaverse, especially as a B2B strategy, has an important role to play in an organizations' strategy.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>Many businesses are making investments in metaverse. They should continue.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Social implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>Metaverse impacts extends beyond B2C applications into the B2B workplace.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality and value</jats:title>
<jats:p>This work is completely original, based on new data and analysis that has not been published elsewhere.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Metaverse: the post--hype future

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although entrepreneurial failure has primarily been examined through recovery and learning perspectives, considerably less attention has been devoted to understanding how failure may contribute to future leadership capital. Drawing on experiential learning theory, intellectual capital theory and signaling theory, this study aims to develop and test a framework explaining how entrepreneurial failure contributes to entrepreneurial leadership capital through experiential learning processes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study uses survey data collected from 736 entrepreneurs across France, Germany, the United Arab Emirates, Lebanon and Saudi Arabia. The hypotheses were tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings show that entrepreneurial failure positively influences experiential learning, which subsequently strengthens entrepreneurial leadership capital. Entrepreneurial leadership capital further increases investor confidence and team commitment in subsequent ventures. The results also demonstrate that intelligent failure strengthens the relationship between entrepreneurial failure and experiential learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study introduces entrepreneurial leadership capital as a distinct form of intangible strategic capital emerging through adversity-driven learning. The findings suggest that entrepreneurial failure may strengthen future legitimacy and stakeholder confidence when entrepreneurs transform adversity into adaptive leadership capability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: From failure to leadership capital: how entrepreneurial setbacks build founder value

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how Chief Financial Officers (CFOs) use strategic financial storytelling to transform quantitative financial information into narratives that align stakeholders with long-term organizational strategy. Although prior research has focused on financial reporting and impression management, limited attention has been given to storytelling as a strategic leadership capability for organizational sensemaking and stakeholder alignment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative narrative inquiry approach was employed using semi-structured interviews with 20 CFOs and senior finance executives from the entertainment industry. Data were analyzed through template analysis within a multi-theoretical framework integrating Systems Thinking, Stakeholder Communication Theory, Rhetorical Theory of Strategy, Strategic Fit Theory, Institutional Theory, and Sensemaking Theory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings identify seven strategic financial storytelling practices, including aligning financial narratives with long-term strategy, connecting performance to organizational purpose, translating strategy through KPI and trend narratives, integrating operational risks and opportunities, fostering cross-functional ownership, framing short-term costs as long-term value, and building stakeholder trust through transparent communication. These practices demonstrate that financial storytelling enables CFOs to move beyond financial reporting toward strategic leadership and organizational alignment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study introduces Strategic Financial Storytelling as a leadership capability supported by an integrated six-theory framework. It advances strategy and leadership research by showing how storytelling strengthens strategic alignment, stakeholder trust, organizational sensemaking, and executive communication while offering a practical framework for senior leaders.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Vision through numbers: strategic financial storytelling and sensemaking in leadership communication

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper examines how trust shapes the enactment and retrospective evaluation of compassionate leadership through the analysis of leaders’ real-time retrospective negotiations. Through interactional analysis of leadership meetings in a Turkish manufacturing firm, it shows that compassionate leadership is a relational practice that carries reputational and organisational risk when trust-based compassionate acts do not produce the expected response. More specifically, the paper examines how business partners retrospectively negotiate responsibility after one of the founders’ compassionate act results in perceived betrayal, financial loss and reputational vulnerability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study adopts an ethnographically informed qualitative design and analyses naturally occurring workplace interaction from strategic meetings between business partners. Using interactional sociolinguistic tools, the paper examines how participants collaboratively reconstruct the incident, assign blame, manage face, and renegotiate expectations regarding appropriate leadership conduct and future trust relations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings show that while trust acts as a precondition of showing compassion, when this retrospectively proves misplaced it may transform compassion into perceived managerial weakness or naivety. Although the founder explicitly constructs himself as compassionate and well-intentioned, colleagues partially attribute responsibility to him for trusting the employee, thereby questioning his managerial judgement and symbolic authority. The analysis demonstrates that compassionate leadership involves not only emotional labour, but also interpersonal, reputational, and organisational risk when trust proves misplaced.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper makes a theoretical contribution to literature, by integrating trust into the compassion process and conceptualising it as a central element of compassionate appraisal.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Trust as a precondition for compassionate leadership: a discourse analytical perspective

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although strategic imitations can erode the competitiveness of firms, there has been limited conceptualization of the different pathways through which imitation can lead to various types of business failures. This study examines mechanisms through which different types of imitations can lead to business failure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Several scientific databases were searched to elicit insights for the conceptualization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper advances a four-domain organizing framework to elucidate the imitation-failure (I-F) nexus: imitation strategy (process imitation vs. product imitation) and the nature and speed of imitation-induced business failure (incremental failure vs. sudden failure).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper is valuable for academics and practitioners in providing managerial and policy implications along with directions for future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The amalgamation of these two vital streams of research culminates in the development of a unified framework that provides much-needed insights into imitation-induced business failure, the challenges that illuminate the life cycle of firms, and their organizational prospects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Strategic imitation-business failure nexus
