strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>The unfolding story of Boeing enables increased understanding of what transpired, of how what happened. That understanding enables fuller, more nuanced, specific, and useful recommendations for organizational leaders everywhere.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>Compiling key events in Boeing’s migration from symbol of acclaimed quality products to a troubled maker of a repeatedly (and fatally so) flawed product ground interpretation and extraction of lessons for organizational leaders.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>Restoring Boeing’s legacy of trust and industry leadership would demand more than words. It will demand rethinking strategic direction and implementation, such as restructuring its work systems, particularly the decision-making processes, and aligning them with long-term goals of quality, safety, and innovation. Boeing needs a coordinated effort to rebuild its culture, an effort necessarily comparable to the effort it employed to disassemble it.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>This paper assists readers in understanding what underlies the Boeing story, indeed the Boeing tragedy. The facts testify to the decay and rot at Boeing. The facts alone, even when combined with first pass “sense making” under headings such as “culture” and “short term focus”, do not adequately explain what produced the facts. This paper attempts to provide that explanation in the service of furthering learning and improving future actions by organizational leaders, especially concerning their development and implementation of strategy.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>Boeing offers a cautionary tale-fatality, destruction of value, and erosion of employee well-being. Organizing this tale, as the article does, through both application of theory and extraction of lessons, moves the tale beyond frightening to understanding of underlying leadership and of how to avoid replicating Boeing's tragedy.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>This paper assists readers in understanding what underlies the Boeing story, indeed the Boeing tragedy. The facts testify to the decay and rot at Boeing. The facts alone, even when combined with first pass “sense making” under headings such as “culture” and “short term focus”, do not sufficiently explain what produced the facts. This paper attempts to provide that explanation in the service of furthering learning and improving future actions by organizational leaders, especially concerning their development and implementation of strategy.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>This paper critically examines the distributed leadership literature, identifying its conceptual foundations, thematic developments, and research gaps. Synthesizing existing studies aims to advance theoretical and practical understandings of distributed leadership across diverse contexts.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>A rigorous three-step systematic literature review (SLR) process was employed to analyze 111 peer-reviewed studies published between 2002 and 2022. This approach integrates descriptive and thematic analyses to address key research questions on distributed leadership's conceptualization, thematic trends, and research gaps.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>The review highlights distributed leadership as a dynamic and context-dependent concept, emphasizing its social, collaborative, and performance-driven dimensions. Three primary themes emerged: behavioral perspectives, contextual influences, and performance implications. Gaps were identified in empirical, theoretical, population, and methodological domains. These include insufficient research in noneducational sectors, limited exploration of distributed leadership's applicability in developing nations, and the need for empirically validated frameworks and qualitative methodologies.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>This review is among the first to systematically map distributed leadership's evolution across multiple contexts using an SLR approach. It provides a robust synthesis of the field, offering a validated baseline for future research. The study's methodological rigor and its focus on underexplored areas contribute significantly to advancing the discourse on distributed leadership.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Distributed leadership: a systematic literature review

<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>This study proposes a theoretical model linking leadership and followership styles.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>A new instrument was developed and tested on 271 respondents from Armenia, Denmark, Germany, and the USA. Factor analysis identified three leadership styles (autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire) and three followership styles (compliant, collaborating, initiating).</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>The results showed that autocratic leadership was positively associated with compliant followership, and democratic leadership was positively associated with collaborating followership. No correlation was found between laissez-faire leadership and initiating followership. However, collaborative followership was positively associated with all three leadership styles.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>This study contributes a new theoretical model and a novel instrument for measuring the interplay between leadership and followership styles, offering fresh insights into leadership dynamics.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Linking leadership and followership styles

<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>Dissolving industry boundaries, coupled with an increasing need for collaboration and mutual adaptation, necessitates the adoption of diverse innovation concepts and flexible management practices. While organizations are striving to be agile and receptive, prioritizing flexibility over meticulous planning, the strategies required to achieve these outcomes remain underdeveloped.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>Between 2019 and 2022, 100 peer-reviewed papers were reviewed to identify 68 agile practices, forming the basis for the classification. A conceptual-to-empirical approach led to the framework's development, involving 40 expert interviews and nine focus groups with participants from different countries from 2020 to 2023. These interactions validated the framework's dimensions and real-world applicability.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>The study revealed that inter-organizational agility serves as a catalyst, effectively harmonizing open and frugal innovation to address market and customer constraints. This framework offers managers a valuable tool for navigating uncertainties and ambiguities and creating and capturing value within open innovation ecosystems that go beyond transient competitive advantages.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>The case study suggests co-innovation and bricolage as novel managerial capabilities that foster innovation, mainly when supported by inter-organizational agility. It provides insights into distinguishing between various forms of agility through a multidimensional framework.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>The study provided crucial insights into the necessity for agility in complex and uncertain environments. Through the integration of frugal and open innovation approaches in co-innovation, inter-organizational agility is presented as a framework for achieving both transient competitive advantage and sustainable innovation power.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Leveraging inter-organizational agility for innovation

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>If purpose represents an organization’s reason for being, it should have significant implications for everyone involved, from top executives and leadership teams to employees and external stakeholders. Yet, how purpose connects the critical human and institutional components of an organization remains insufficiently addressed in the literature. The aim of the current text is to advance a circular model of organizational purpose focused on internal stakeholders, namely employees, managers, and leaders.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At the corporate level, purpose is typically conceptualized as an organizational attribute, akin to vision, mission, and values. This anthropomorphic framing is useful because it helps scientists and managers understand what purpose is, where it originates, and why it matters. However, attributing individual-level characteristics to an organization has limitations when explaining how purpose is created and how it is intended to influence employees and managers. The current text advances a conceptual model aimed at addressing these limitations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The text first integrates individual purpose with organizational purpose, arguing that the closer the fit between the two, the greater the likelihood that the organization will generate value. It then introduces a cycle that connects organizational actors in the design and implementation of corporate purpose. This circular model seeks to enhance alignment between the purpose of the company’s founders and/or top management team and the individual purposes of employees and other stakeholders.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As rapid technological change and shifts in the world of work create new complexities for individuals, companies, and society, organizational purpose is emerging as a critical theme; this text contends that a well-defined purpose can offer meaning and direction to all stakeholders, from employees to top management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The purpose effect: connecting hearts, minds and management

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Police Leadership Commission was established to provide a framework for the future of policing leadership in England and Wales through a comprehensive review of existing practices which engaged policing professionals and stakeholders. The present paper critically analyzes the final report of the Commission, arguing that it represents a missed opportunity to engender sustainable change.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This structured policy analysis uses theories of autonomous motivation and organizational behavior, amongst others, to analyze the final report and identify tensions between its recommendations and their likely effects. Including the potential consequences of this for the achievement of human sustainability in policing and the forthcoming major structural and strategic reform.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>It is proposed that the Police Leadership Commission is unlikely to result in notable change in practices due to limited attention to the underlying cultures which serve to drive these, particularly those which constrain employee autonomy, perpetuate mistrust, and contribute to perceived organizational injustices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Through analyzing contemporary policing leadership strategy the present article makes an original contribution to scholarship in identifying subliminal themes which repeatedly serve to thwart change in the sector. Many of which will be relevant to others providing public and private professional services, where strong organizational or occupational cultures thrive, or where hierarchical traditions and rules-based climates perpetuate.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The missed opportunities of the England and Wales police leadership commission

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This article examines leadership from a governance perspective, focusing on how leadership operates within organizational systems rather than how it is typically described in behavioral terms. It investigates how coordination, accountability translation and trust building are enacted in practice and how they relate to organizational performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study draws on an analysis of organizational disclosures from large publicly listed firms over the period 2016 to 2023. Governance functions are identified through structured coding of annual reports and Form 10-K filings. Panel regression with firm and year fixed effects is used to examine the relationship between these functions and firm performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings show that governance functions are observable and measurable in organizational disclosures, but do not operate as independent drivers of performance. Coordination exhibits a consistent positive directional association with performance, indicating that alignment and integration may support organizational effectiveness but do not operate as an independent statistically significant effect. Accountability translation does not show a direct relationship with performance, suggesting that its contribution lies in organizational discipline and stability. Trust building shows a negative but statistically insignificant association with performance, indicating that legitimacy oriented practices may not translate directly into short term financial outcomes. Overall, the results indicate that governance functions operate as an interdependent system rather than as isolated effects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study relies on disclosure-based measures that capture how governance is articulated rather than fully enacted in practice. The sample is limited to large publicly listed firms and the findings are observational. Future research should examine governance enactment using alternative data sources, larger samples and longitudinal or mixed-method designs to further evaluate the proposed framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article provides a framework for diagnosing governance effectiveness in practice. Organizations can assess leadership by examining alignment across units, the embedding of accountability into routines and the credibility of stakeholder engagement. The findings suggest that improving governance requires balancing these functions rather than focusing on any single dimension.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Understanding leadership as governance highlights the importance of transparent decision-making, embedded accountability and stakeholder trust in sustaining responsible organizations. Strengthening these governance functions can enhance organizational legitimacy, stakeholder confidence and broader institutional effectiveness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study connects leadership and governance by conceptualizing leadership as a mechanism through which governance is enacted in practice. It moves beyond leadership style to identify specific organizational functions that can be observed, measured and improved.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Leadership as governance in practice: coordination, accountability and trust in organizational performance

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research shows that intangible assets play a vital role in early-stage digital platform joint ventures, but they must be carefully managed to maintain their positive impact.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study follows a multi-case study approach in the European automotive industry.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study identifies (1) Digital platform know-how, (2) Marketing Assets, and (3) Core platform data as three critical intangible assets to effectively integrate to establish a sustainable platform ecosystem. All three assets can be critical for platform success, but relate to different stages of platform maturity and the type of platform. Furthermore, we identify two types of risks associated with intangible assets that may harm the platform owner (strategic risks) or those that threaten the success of the platform endeavor (cooperation risk). Last, our research shows that the number and diversity of joint venture partners are decisive for the stability and success of the entire platform.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This work contributes to digital platform research by providing a framework to help joint ventures select relevant assets and partner configurations while monitoring the risks associated with sharing these assets. We thus broaden the picture in digital platform research by deepening the understanding of resource requirements along the development process of digital platforms. Furthermore, we contribute to coopetition research by adding a multi-sided platform perspective to a primarily two-sided conceptualization of this research landscape.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research provides managers with insights into the digital platform know-how, marketing assets, and core platform data are essential to build platforms. Additionally, we highlight the associated risks and offer evidence-based examples of effective implementation practices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Existing research on digital platforms predominantly centers on platform-native firms, despite the growing practical significance of platforms developed by incumbent firms. While incumbents often engage in cooperative strategies during platform development, the influence of intangible assets in this context remains underexplored in the academic literature.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Incumbent joint ventures in digital platforms: exploring the role of intangible assets

<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>This paper investigates the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in personal financial management, focusing on its potential to enhance financial decision-making while highlighting associated ethical, regulatory, and accessibility challenges.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>A structured literature review methodology was employed, incorporating peer-reviewed academic publications, industry reports, and policy papers published between 2019 and early 2025. The review synthesizes insights across different thematic domains including investment management, digital inclusion, algorithmic bias, and AI explainability.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>AI significantly enhances personal financial services by automating tasks, customizing investment strategies, and improving financial literacy. However, ethical risks, such as algorithmic bias, automation bias, and data privacy violations, can exacerbate existing inequalities. Transparency, fairness-aware machine learning, and inclusive design are essential for responsible AI integration.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>The findings offer guidance for designing user-centric, ethical, and accessible AI financial services. Recommendations include integrating explainable AI tools, enhancing digital literacy programs, and adopting corporate digital responsibility frameworks.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Social implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>If designed responsibly, AI can democratize financial services, improve financial wellbeing, and promote inclusion. However, without ethical safeguards, it risks reinforcing systemic biases and excluding vulnerable populations. Bridging the digital divide and ensuring regulatory oversight are vital to ensuring equitable outcomes.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>This study provides a comprehensive synthesis of current debates and emerging practices surrounding AI in personal finance. It highlights a unique intersection of technological innovation and ethical responsibility, contributing to ongoing discourse on sustainable and inclusive digital finance.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Navigating the AI-driven transformation of personal finance: opportunities, challenges, and ethical imperatives

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper examines a persistent problem in organisations: leadership is often understood as relational or practice-based, while the organisational conditions that sustain coordination, accountability and participation remain under-specified. It aims to reconceptualise leadership as governance practice, focusing on how leadership is organised and stabilised through everyday organisational arrangements.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper adopts a conceptual approach, drawing on leadership-as-practice, governance and organisation studies literature. It develops an integrative framework that connects relational leadership processes with governance arrangements, focusing on coordination, accountability translation and participation as key organising dimensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper shows that leadership is not simply enacted through interaction but is constituted through governance practices that organise coordination, structure accountability and shape participation. It demonstrates how leadership becomes stabilised and extended across time and space through these arrangements rather than remaining confined to local interaction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper is conceptual and does not include empirical analysis. It highlights the need for future research examining how governance arrangements shape leadership processes across organisational contexts and how these arrangements influence power, participation and accountability in practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper suggests that leaders should focus less on influencing individuals and more on designing governance arrangements that enable coordination, clarify accountability and support meaningful participation. It highlights how weak governance structures can undermine leadership effectiveness even when relational processes are strong.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By showing how participation and accountability are structured through governance, the paper highlights how leadership practices shape inclusion, voice and the experience of meaningful work. It points to the uneven distribution of participation and recognition within organisations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper offers a novel integration of leadership and governance by conceptualising leadership as governance practice. It moves beyond treating governance as context and instead positions it as the medium through which leadership is constituted, providing a new way of understanding how collective action is organised.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Why leadership fails without governance: rethinking coordination, accountability and participation in organisations

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A purpose without an ethical foundation risks can become self-serving or even harmful, whereas ethical frameworks help ensure that leadership serves the broader community. This paper aims to develop a framework that links ethical principles to organizational practices in contemporary leadership. Drawing on utilitarian, justice, and virtue perspectives on ethics, the paper integrates these with scriptural insights from the Jewish tradition, particularly the Abrahamic narrative. In doing so, it explores how ethical principles can inform purpose-driven leadership and guide organizations in navigating today’s societal and strategic challenges.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This conceptual paper integrates three ethical perspectives with contemporary management theories (e.g., stakeholder theory, purpose-driven leadership) and applies them across seven principle–application linkages. Each linkage follows a structured logic: ethical justifications, scriptural illustrations grounded in the Jewish tradition, and managerial applications. This approach bridges moral philosophy and organizational practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The research indicates that ethical perspectives can be systematically translated into organizational practices through a principle–application framework. The integration of ethical theory, scriptural narrative, and management concepts suggests that purpose-driven leadership is grounded in stewardship, justice, compassion, and integrity. Organizations that align their strategies with these principles can achieve sustainable performance, build stakeholder trust, and address complex societal challenges.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Management theories often emphasize efficiency, organizational behavior, and strategic decision-making, which are important for operational success. However, they tend to be pragmatic and context-specific, focusing more on how to manage than on why leadership exists and what constitutes a morally sound purpose. This paper mitigates the gap by examining contemporary management research alongside ethical principles rooted in Abrahamic traditions, an approach that remains underexplored in leadership studies. By combining traditional ethical insights with modern business imperatives, the paper offers both theoretical depth and practical, societal relevance for leaders who seek to build purpose into their organizational culture.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: A principle–application framework for purpose-driven leadership and organizations

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study determined the characteristics and behaviors of leaders leading a digitalization that their followers find effective. In addition, the research also found empirical evidence on how effective leadership amid digitalization shaped followers’ attitudes and behaviors that then impacts the team outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study used a qualitative approach. Data were gathered using focus group discussions (FGDs) with teams that have recently gone through digitalization. Eleven FGDs, with 3 members per FGD, were completed among teams in Philippine-based organizations. Content analysis was used to analyze the data collected to understand the followers’ perspectives on leadership during digitalization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study reports effective leadership characteristics (firm, considerate and trusting, has technological familiarity and hands-on) and behaviors (fosters collaboration and communication, motivates and empowers, supports and mentors and manages change effectively) perceived by the followers as essential in a digitalization. Demonstrating effective leadership influenced the followers’ attitudes and behaviors by feeling inspired, motivated, and having a positive work attitude. As a team-level outcome, the digitalization produced results, improved team dynamics, enhanced accountability and ownership, ensured personal & professional growth, and improved morale and job satisfaction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results highlighted how being hands-on leaders that possess effective leadership characteristics and behaviors are enough. During digitalization, the leader is expected to be familiar with technology (characteristic) and can manage changes effectively (behavior). By ensuring leaders possess these additional characteristics and behavior, it can help dramatically increase the chances of the digitalization to be completed successfully and achieve positive outcomes as stated in this research. Organizations can prepare leaders to lead digitalization by ensuring these leaders will get technical and change management training.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study sought to contribute to the relatively limited literature on understanding leadership from the follower’s perspective. This study is important because the future technological advancement will introduce a form of digitalization at any level in organizations. The results highlight the need to cultivate characteristics such as fosters collaboration and communication, motivates and empowers, supports and mentors, manages change effectively, and behaviors that are considerate and trusting, firm, familiar with technology, and being hands-on to fully become an effective leader in leading any digitalization in large enterprises in the Philippine setting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Leading digitalization from the follower’s perspective

<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>The paper explores the evolution of the sharing economy, particularly focusing on the growing regulatory constraints and societal pushback. With platforms like Airbnb and Uber at the forefront, the paper investigates how these businesses, which initially thrived in an unregulated environment, are now facing tighter regulations and changing market conditions. It also examines potential future scenarios and strategic adaptations needed for the sharing economy to sustain its performance amid these emerging challenges.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>This article is an opinion piece based on secondary data sources. It analyzes the sharing economy's evolution by reviewing regulatory changes, competitive pressures, and societal responses.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>The sharing economy has reached significant boundaries due to evolving regulatory frameworks and increasing societal pushback. Examples include Barcelona's ban on short-term rentals and the U.S. Department of Labor's reclassification of gig workers. These changes indicate a shift in how these platforms operate, requiring new strategies to adapt to these pressures, such as increased transparency, partnerships with local governments, and environmental sustainability initiatives.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>The paper contributes to the ongoing discussion on the future of the sharing economy by highlighting its current boundary conditions, particularly focusing on regulatory developments and societal concerns. It offers unique insights into potential future adaptations and scenarios for platforms to sustain growth, making it relevant for both academics and practitioners interested in platform strategies and regulatory environments.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: The sharing economy reaching its boundaries: What’s Next?

<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>This paper seeks to identify a rounded understanding of two fuzzy terms in wide but muddled use in guiding corporate leadership: accountability and responsibility. Both have deep resonance discussions of strategy and corporate affairs, but their often-confused meanings both inform actions and impede understanding. Each has normative implications for the practice of corporate governance, and yet each, like an empty vessel,[1] leaves practitioners with an unhappy sense of knowing they have a use but not knowing what to do with them.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>This essay examines the varied uses of these terms in academic literature and practitioner discussions, exploring their conflicting meanings through lenses of philosophy, literary writing, and management studies to show how each, in their flux, overlap and diverge.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>The article analyses themes obscured by these muddy waters and clarifies them by speculating on how their ambiguity demands reflexive, thoughtful action and interaction between the parties in absence of clear hierarchy of command or greater authority. How meaningful that interaction is questionable, when the words are so full of meanings without an iterative process of understanding.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>Given the prevalence of the ambiguities is usage, clarifying terms is not a realistic option. Instead, this essay proposes that insofar as these concepts reflect <jats:italic>abilities,</jats:italic> they represent our ability to embrace their ambiguity in a philosophically pragmatic way, and in so doing be able to act accountably and responsibly.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Filling empty vessels: accountability, responsibility, and corporate leadership

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This article helps executives determine when a firm’s legacy can support transformation and which constraint is preventing progress and must be resolved first.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article develops a practitioner diagnostic – the Legacy Multiplier – by integrating strategy, corporate heritage, complementarity and platform insights with illustrative case evidence from legacy-firm renewal and failure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Legacy firms rarely fail because they lack assets. They often stall because inherited assets remain disconnected. The framework identifies three viability conditions and five interdependent levers – narrative capital, organizational networks, adjacent value pools, value architecture and platform infrastructure. When aligned these levers can reinforce one another. A blocking-lever logic helps leaders identify the constraint preventing progress.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework is an interpretive practitioner diagnostic; its causal claims require future empirical testing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The diagnostic helps leadership teams shift from asking “what should we do next?” to “what must be fixed first?”</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article reframes legacy as a system-activation challenge and provides an executive tool for diagnosing when heritage supports renewal, when it constrains it and how to sequence action.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Stop escaping your past. How leaders turn legacy into a self-reinforcing advantage

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study tests the operationalization of environmental and social sustainability accounting practices (ESAP) in the manufacturing sector and evaluates how internal and external governance mechanisms shape its adoption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Grounded in stakeholder theory, this study employs advanced analytical approaches, specifically partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) alongside probit estimation, to examine the factors shaping ESAP adoption across a sample of 200 manufacturing firms in Ghana.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that although ESAP adoption remains modest, manufacturing firms more readily deploy activity-based costing (ABC), environmental management accounting (EMA) and lifecycle costing than customer profitability analysis or competitor accounting. Internal governance mechanisms, particularly IT capability, accounting department structure, and strategic orientation, significantly shape ESAP implementation. Externally, only market competition intensity exerts a discernible influence, with market orientation and environmental uncertainty proving negligible. Collectively, these findings underscore how governance architectures condition firms’ capacity to embed sustainability accounting within strategic imperatives and align with evolving stakeholder demands.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study contributes new empirical evidence on governance-driven sustainability accounting in a developing-country manufacturing context, an under-researched domain. It highlights the primacy of internal governance capabilities and market competition over conventional external pressures, offering a contextualized understanding of ESAP adoption in countries with weak regulatory environments. The findings inform policymakers, regulators and corporate leaders about structuring governance mechanisms to advance sustainability accounting and align with SDGs in emerging economies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Exploring governance-driven sustainability accounting in a developing economy

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Examine how task conflict (TC) influences employee creativity (EC) and organizational commitment (OC), and whether leaders’ competitive and cooperative conflict management styles differentially moderate these effects in Vietnamese IT firms, drawing on Social Exchange Theory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional survey of IT project employees in Vietnam was conducted using validated measures of TC, EC, OC, and competitive and cooperative conflict management styles. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS–SEM) was used to test reliability/validity, direct paths, moderation, and predictive power through bootstrapping.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>TC was negatively associated with both EC and OC, while OC was positively associated with EC. Two novel results emerged: competitive conflict management styles intensified the negative association between TC and EC, whereas cooperative conflict management styles attenuated the negative association between TC and OC. The model explained substantial variance in both outcomes and demonstrated good predictive relevance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Evidence from this study cautions against the assumption that increasing debate necessarily promotes idea generation. Leaders’ competitive style (COM) is associated with reduced EC, whereas a cooperative style (COO) helps preserve OC under TC. Accordingly, organizations should (i) equip leaders to diagnose task tensions, (ii) institutionalize psychological safety practices, and (iii) match conflict management styles to the specific outcome to be safeguarded, avoiding competitive conflict management styles when creativity is paramount and prioritizing cooperative conflict management styles to maintain commitment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Introduces evidence of differentiated moderation in a collectivist, knowledge-intensive context, integrating EC and OC within a single framework and clarifying when specific conflict styles exacerbate or buffer the harms of conflict.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Managing task conflict for employee creativity and organizational commitment: competitive versus cooperative

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to address a strategic leadership dilemma by asking when profitability translates into credible sustainability reporting. It examines whether board governance conditions the relationship between financial capacity and higher levels of sustainability-reporting credibility among manufacturing firms in Africa.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study uses a balanced panel of 201 firms observed from 2014 to 2023, yielding 2,010 firm-year observations. Sustainability reporting credibility (SRC) is hand-coded as an ordinal ladder ranging from no identifiable disclosure to board-governed and externally assured reporting. Correlated random-effects ordered-logit models with firm-clustered standard errors are used, supplemented by linear-panel and measurement sensitivity tests.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Board size and average director tenure are positively associated with higher credibility stages, whereas female board representation and the non-executive director ratio are not statistically significant. Return on equity is not independently significant in the direct-effects ordinal model, whereas its association with SRC becomes more positive at higher levels of board size and average director tenure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Senior leaders should treat sustainability-reporting credibility as a strategic governance and control architecture rather than merely as a communication exercise. Financial capacity is more likely to support credible reporting when boards possess sufficient scale, accumulated firm knowledge and oversight capacity to direct resources toward accountability and verification.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study reframes sustainability-reporting credibility as a strategic governance outcome and identifies board governance as a condition that helps convert financial capacity into stronger accountability and verification commitments. It therefore explains not simply whether profitable firms report credibly, but when profitability is more likely to translate into credible sustainability reporting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: When does profitability translate into credible sustainability reporting? The role of board governance

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purposes</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates the strategic bridge-building capabilities (SBBCs) of legitimating agencies (LAs). By focusing on the role of LAs in a faith-based setting, the study examines how these accreditation bodies foster intrasectoral collaboration and advocate for their members’ interests across secular domains and the broader socioeconomic landscape.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Evidence pertaining to LAs was generated through a scoping review, enabling primary data collection to commence with a survey. Survey responses informed the purposive selection of four LAs and fourteen affiliated organizations for in-depth study. Insights were further enriched through online interviews and focus group discussions involving sixty-four senior officials.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings reveal ten contemporary roles fulfilled by LAs in the sector examined. Through tailored strategic approaches and multidimensional bridge-building capabilities, these agencies promote convergence and encourage best practices among otherwise autonomous entities. Moreover, their activities exert a legitimating influence within the social sphere and play a pivotal role in advancing member congregations’ revitalization agendas.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>It is anticipated that legitimating agency leaders and their affiliates will be inspired to adopt a more strategically oriented perspective on their roles, fostering more effective stakeholder relationship management and driving improvements in overall organizational performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to the literature on LAs. By addressing a significant gap in understanding the SBBCs of these accreditation organizations, it aims to shed light on how their functions enable constituents to navigate operational challenges intensified by legitimation struggles.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Unpacking the strategic bridge-building capabilities of legitimating agencies

                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Asynchronous interactions pervade global teams, yet how time delays shape leadership remains underexplored. This study examines temporal distance – the delay between leader–follower interactions – as a boundary condition moderating leadership effectiveness in global virtual teams, developing a framework for asynchronous leadership adaptations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An integrative review synthesized 82 multidisciplinary studies on virtual leadership and asynchronous team coordination, using multilevel categorization (micro, meso, macro) with systematic clustering of temporal mechanisms and boundary conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Temporal distance systematically moderates leadership transmission: the effectiveness of task-oriented behaviors appears to remain robust under delay, whereas relationship-oriented behaviors weaken; temporal adaptability and virtual relationship quality buffer these losses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework’s primary focus is on globally distributed teams with significant time zone separation; applicability to hybrid or local asynchronous teams may be limited, suggesting need for future research extensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Beyond improving team coordination, the framework provides actionable insights for global organizational strategic management by enabling leaders to design temporally resilient structures that enhance collaboration, retention, and competitive agility in multinational contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Enhanced temporal leadership promotes inclusive global work environments by overcoming geographic and temporal barriers to participation and career growth.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Unlike previous research treating temporal aspects as secondary, this study positions temporal distance as a significant boundary condition requiring distinct leadership adaptations. The framework advances virtual leadership theory by explaining previously inconsistent findings and identifying mechanisms through which time separation moderates leadership processes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Leading across time zones: a strategic framework for leading virtual teams in global organizations

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In the present study, we develop and validate the Power Addiction Scale (PAS), a reliable and valid scale to assess the compulsive and excessive tendencies to seek, maintain, and exert power among managers and leaders in organizations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first scale to measure power addiction in the field of organizational behavior.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study included 435 employees from Turkey. The scale was developed based on literature review, grouping open-ended responses, expert content validity, pre-testing, administration of the survey, and analysis of data. Analysis methods included exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), reliability analysis using internal consistency, determined by Cronbach’s alpha, and validity analysis using average variance extracted and discriminant validity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The final 29-item scale consisted of two dimensions: Power Addicted Behavior and Power Addicted Attitude. The proposed model showed good fit. Reliability, measured through coefficients alpha, was achieved with scores between 0.869 and 0.976. Convergent validity was established through average variance extracted scores greater than 0.50. The power addiction scale also achieved discriminant validity with Machiavellianism, narcissism, and personal need for power.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study developed and validated the first psychometrically sound measure of workplace power addiction, the Power Addiction Scale, thus filling a critical gap in power addiction research. The scale can be practically applied in leadership development, organizational development, and human resource management but needs studies to test cross-cultural validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Conceptualizing and measuring power addiction: scale development and validation

                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper reconceptualizes ethical AI governance as a leadership problem of legitimacy production rather than technical compliance. Existing frameworks presume stable infrastructure, coherent institutions, and baseline trust − assumptions that frequently fail in volatile environments. Drawing on Africa as a theory-generating extreme context, this paper reframes ethical governance as a legitimacy infrastructure required for governable AI deployment, addressing the question of who legitimizes the AI algorithm.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper develops an analytically grounded conceptual framework supported by illustrative vignettes. It specifies volatility as three-dimensional: infrastructural, institutional, and socio-political, showing how each generates distinctive governance breakdowns. Building on legitimacy theory and algorithmic accountability scholarship, the paper derives a Sensing–Stabilizing–Legitimizing (SSL) leadership capability model and three falsifiable propositions that explain how organizations sustain contestability and accountability amid instability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In times of volatility, ethical AI governance succeeds only when leaders institutionalize legitimacy infrastructure rather than relying on principles alone. Infrastructural volatility produces exclusion-by-fragility; institutional volatility generates compliance theater; socio-political volatility amplifies legitimacy shocks. The SSL capability chain is decisive for sustaining governable algorithmic authority.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Leaders should establish clear decision rights, escalation pathways, and recourse mechanisms calibrated to volatility conditions. Organizations should build redundancy into monitoring, prioritize safeguards for vulnerable groups, and treat impact assessments as living governance instruments rather than one-time compliance deliverables.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper makes an integrative-conceptual contribution by theorizing volatility as an explicit governance condition and positioning ethical AI governance as a strategic leadership capability rather than a delegated technical task. It positions Africa as an extreme context that reveals hidden assumptions in dominant governance models and generates transferable insights for rising global volatility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Who legitimises the AI algorithm? Leadership, volatility and the governance of algorithmic authority

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study explores the impact of Green HRM Practices and Environmental Sustainability on Employer Branding. It investigates how incorporating Green HRM practices promotes Environmental Sustainability, which creates a positive Employer Brand that attracts younger, environmentally concerned employees.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Based on a quantitative analysis, data was collected from employees working in the Textile and Renewable Energy Sector firms in Pakistan. The data was analyzed using SMART PLS and SPSS.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings reveal that Green HRM practices are not significantly related to Environmental Sustainability. However, Environmental Sustainability is positively related to Employer Branding, with a moderation effect of generational differences between Environmental Sustainability and Employer Branding.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Managers in the textile sector can attract individuals through employer branding. They can advertise and focus on sustainability practices like waste reduction and energy conservation. Managers can integrate environmental criteria into recruitment, training and performance evaluation that will motivates employees to prioritize sustainability in their roles. Top management support for GHRMP builds competencies that foster eco-friendly actions across the workforce and enhance organizational performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In today’s strategically competitive age, organizations aim to have the best talent onboard to ensure optimized performance and productivity while building a sustainable competitive advantage in the long run. On the other hand, sustainability has become a growing concern for organizations, as the young workforce consisting of Millennials and Gen Z prefers organizations that indulge in eco-friendly business practices. The current emphasis on sustainability has had a considerable impact on organizational strategy, especially in the field of green HRM. This study seeks to further advance the previous research. By addressing the gaps in existing literature, the research seeks to provide insight into how Green HRM practices and environmental sustainability initiatives can influence Employer Branding for the companies in the textile and renewable energy sectors in Pakistan.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Architecting future sustainability: explaining the role of green HRM in employer branding

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Contemporary organizations increasingly confront co-occurring demands that differ in urgency, reversibility, ethical salience, and actionability, making assumptions of balance, optimization, or simultaneous accommodation difficult to sustain. This paper reconceptualizes leadership as a process of mediation through which non-commensurable demands are rendered actionable via interpretation, prioritization, ethical justification, and temporal sequencing. In doing so, it addresses a theoretical gap at the intersection of leadership, organizational adaptation, temporality, and ethics. Under asymmetric conditions, leadership effectiveness depends less on structural alignment or capability deployment than on mediation quality − the coherence with which competing demands are sequenced over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper develops an integrative conceptual framework through abductive synthesis across leadership, strategy, sensemaking, paradox, temporality, ethics, organizational process, and attention-based literatures. Drawing on foundational and contemporary scholarship, it theorizes mediation as a distinct process through which leaders construct, justify, and sequence responses to uneven environmental pressures (Joseph et al., 2024; Brielmaier & Friesl, 2023). Sequencing is conceptualized as an ongoing ethically embedded interpretive practice, rather than a structural outcome or coordination device, that becomes increasingly consequential under conditions of non-commensurability. Cross-sector examples illustrate how asymmetric pressures are translated into situated organizational action.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Leadership effectiveness under asymmetric conditions depends less on structural alignment or capability deployment than on the quality of mediation through which competing demands are ordered over time. Organizational outcomes emerge through temporally sequenced patterns of interpretation, prioritization, ethical justification, and action, where early interventions shape subsequent option spaces. As asymmetry intensifies across urgency, reversibility, ethical salience, and actionability, mediation becomes central to sustaining adaptive capacity, organizational legitimacy, and ethical integrity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper makes three novel contributions. First, it introduces environmental asymmetry as a theoretically specified condition in which co-occurring demands differ simultaneously across temporal urgency, reversibility, ethical salience, and actionability − a structural condition that existing frameworks do not adequately theorize. Second, it develops mediation as a distinct processual mechanism through which leaders construct, justify, and sequence responses to non-commensurable demands, thereby advancing beyond equilibrium-oriented accounts of leadership. Third, it theorizes cumulative ethical erosion as a sequencing-driven process structurally distinct from ethical fading, offering a new explanation for why organizations with recognized ethical stakes nonetheless experience moral deterioration over time. Together, these contributions reposition leadership as the disciplined ordering of action when simultaneous accommodation of competing demands is neither feasible nor desirable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Leading between urgency and opportunity: a conceptual lens on asymmetric pressures

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study attempts to explain whether CEO narcissism influences a firm’s strategic distinctiveness. Building on social role theory, the authors also focus on how CEO gender and age moderate the relationship between CEO narcissism and firm’s strategic distinctiveness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The authors conduct two studies to test the hypotheses. Study 1 uses a longitudinal sample of 8,080 firm-year observations of 1,595 unique firms listed in Chinese A-shares from 2006–2018. Study 2 uses cross-sectional data from a survey study of Chinese CEOs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study reveals that narcissistic CEOs’ pursuit of uniqueness and disregard for industry conventions lead them to favor highly distinctive strategic strategy. Besides, female narcissistic CEOs and old narcissistic CEOs have a weaker tendency to adopt distinctive strategy than male narcissistic CEOs and young narcissistic CEOs due to the constraints of role expectations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>First, this study contributes to the narcissism literature by shifting the focus from temporal strategic dynamism to spatial strategic positioning, demonstrating how CEO narcissism drives firms to deviate from industry peers rather than merely changing their own strategy over time. Second, we enrich the antecedents of strategic distinctiveness by identifying narcissism as a core psychological driver, responding to recent calls to explore the underlying motivations for why firms pursue unique strategic positions. Third, by integrating social role theory with upper echelon theory, we provide a more contingent view of the narcissism-strategy link, highlighting how gender and age act as boundary conditions that constrain the expression of a CEO’s narcissistic proclivities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Break the mold: does CEO narcissism affects corporate strategic distinctiveness?

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study attempts to evaluate a theoretical framework explaining the role of servant leadership on followers’ personal branding, where perceived organizational support represents the mediating factor, and job autonomy is the moderating factor.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Servant leadership, personal branding, perceived organizational support, and job autonomy were assessed in an empirical study based on sample of 205 full-time workers working in Jordan. This study used a cross-sectional design due to its quantitative nature, which sought to investigate the relationship between servant leadership, POS, job autonomy, and personal branding. Data were gathered via online survey and analyzed via structural equation modeling (SEM), confirmatory factor analysis, reliability and validity tests, and mediation and moderation tests.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results from SEM reveal that the servant leadership style directly influences follower’s levels of personal branding. Furthermore, the direct relationship between servant leadership and personal branding was found to be mediated by employees’ perceptions of perceived organizational support. Finally, job autonomy moderates this relationship, suggesting that followers who are working on low autonomy tasks have lower personal branding.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results. First, the research focus on specific sectors which limits the ability to generalize the findings into other contexts. Second, since the valuation and utilization of resources are conditioned by cultural and institutional contexts, future studies could replicate the model of the study in other national contexts. Finally, the use of cross-sectional design restricts the ability to make the inferences of causality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides contribution in three major aspects. First, it highlights servant leadership as a relational resource that employees can leverage to enhance personal branding through perceived organizational support. Second, proposed moderated mediation results support the presence of nonlinear resource gain spirals, which are more dynamic than additive, hence addressing the most recent calls to investigate interactive resource dynamics in the framework. Third, it provides empirical support for cultural contingency of resource processes, thus responding to demands of non-Western validation of organizational theories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study is distinctive as it is one of the first studies that tested the influence of servant leadership and personal branding through perceived organizational support and job autonomy within a Jordanian context.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Servant leadership and its relation to personal branding: testing a mediated-moderated model

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Performance appraisals have persisted for over a century yet continue generating negative employee reactions despite extensive research and refinement efforts. This study examines how meta-communication, the communication about organizational processes themselves, influences employee decision-making regarding performance appraisal responses and behaviors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on systematic thematic analysis of 45 semi-structured interviews, we analyzed how informal communications create parallel decision-making frameworks that influence employee responses to formal evaluation systems by integrating Psychological Contract Theory, Meta-communication Theory, and Social Capital Theory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four interconnected meta-communicative processes were identified: a performance appraisal paradox driven by rhetoric-reality gaps; social capital networks functioning as parallel decision-making systems; multi-layered communication decoding strategies; and systematic accommodation withdrawal patterns that signal conditional organizational acceptance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Several limitations affect generalizability. Single-country focus limits international generalizability, particularly given cultural differences in communication styles, power distance orientations (Hofstede, 2011). The cross-sectional design cannot capture longitudinal decision-making processes or meta-communication memory pattern evolution. The qualitative methodology, whilst appropriate for understanding subjective decision-making processes, limits statistical generalization and the ability to quantify relationships between variables (Drisko, 2024). Snowball sampling may have created some homogeneity in perspectives, potentially over-representing employees with negative performance appraisal experiences. The study’s focus on meta-communicative processes may underemphasize other factors influencing employee decision-making, such as individual personality differences, organizational culture variations, or industry-specific considerations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Meta-communicative channels create compound effects across cognitive, communicative, and relational domains that cannot be predicted through single-theory approaches. The research demonstrates that performance appraisal effectiveness depends on broader communicative ecosystems that extend beyond manager-employee interactions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper makes a dual contribution. Theoretically, it introduces the Integrated Promise-Performance Framework (IPPF), synthesizing Psychological Contract, Meta-communication, and Social Capital theories to explain how informal communications shape employee responses to performance appraisals. Practically, it equips HR professionals and line managers with tools for diagnosing performance management breakdown through meta-communicative memory awareness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: When promises fail: social networks and employee responses to performance appraisals

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to examine the mechanisms through which employee psychological entitlement influence emotional exhaustion and abusive supervision among team managers, and its impact on team cohesion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on Conservation of Resources theory, this study investigated the relationships among team members’ psychological entitlement (PE), counterproductive workplace behavior (CWB), team managers’ emotional exhaustion (EE) and abusive supervision (AS), and team cohesion (TC). Adopting a dyadic conceptual approach, Study 1 examined these relationships from the perspective of team managers, while Study 2 investigated them from the perspective of team members. Specifically, this study hypothesized that CWB mediates the relationships between PE and EE/TC (Study 1), and between PE and AS (Study 2).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings revealed that while manager-perceived PE positively correlated with CWB (Study 1), self-reported data showed a nonsignificant relationship (Study 2), highlighting the critical role of perspective. Crucially, CWB emerged as a significant mediator: it mediated the relationships between PE and team managers’ emotional exhaustion and team cohesion (Study 1), and between PE and team managers’ abusive supervision (Study 2). Interestingly, the direct impact of PE on emotional exhaustion and team cohesion was nonsignificant, suggesting CWB acts as the critical link.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings suggest that organizations should prioritize identifying and managing CWB, given its significant burden on team resources and dynamics. It is also crucial to address the root causes of managerial abusive supervision, recognizing it can stem from resource depletion and lack of support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes by adopting a novel dyadic conceptual approach to examine psychological entitlement and its impact from both manager and member perspectives, grounded in COR theory. It highlights CWB as a critical mediator, explaining how team members’ entitlement influences managerial well-being and team dynamics, including the emergence of abusive supervision as a manager’s maladaptive coping mechanism.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Psychological entitlement and its impact on teams: a resource perspective on manager-member dynamics
