strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper challenges the perceived antagonism between strategic leadership and compassionate leadership. It argues that the tension is not inevitable in organizational decision-making, but arises from essentialist assumptions that treat strategy and compassion as fixed leadership attributes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scholarly essay develops a conceptual argument grounded in social constructionist and attributional perspectives on leadership. Organizational episodes are used illustratively, rather than as empirical cases, to show how leadership discourse and observer interpretation can produce and stabilize the apparent conflict between strategic and compassionate leadership.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Two leadership myths are identified: that strategy requires emotional distance and that compassion undermines strategic resolve. These myths are sustained through attributional habits, institutional reinforcement, professional socialization, and psychological defense. When leadership is reframed as interpretive rather than essential, the perceived incompatibility diminishes. Integration is shown to be provisional, audience-dependent, and contingent upon interpretation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>People in leadership positions cannot ensure that their actions will be interpreted as both strategically necessary and compassionately enacted, although framing, communication, and attention to process can influence those judgments. More broadly, organizations, leadership development, and leadership scholarship can challenge the categories that present strategic resolve and compassion as opposing qualities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper reframes leadership as a site of ongoing public judgment, where authority and morality are continually contested rather than inherently possessed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper applies a non-essentialist account of leadership to the strategy-compassion dilemma. It relocates the problem from how people in leadership positions balance supposedly competing qualities to how observers interpret the same action as strategic, compassionate, both, or neither. Reconciliation is therefore reframed as a provisional interpretive judgment rather than an integration of leadership attributes within the individual.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Damned if you do, damned if you don’t: the interpretive dilemma of strategic and compassionate leadership

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As organizations leverage advanced digital technologies to drive sustainability – a convergence recognized as the “twin transition” – they face heterogeneous and conditional risks. This paper addresses the “AI-Green Paradox,” wherein opaque or biased algorithms can inadvertently undermine environmental, social, and governance (ESG) outcomes. It aims to provide executives with a “Responsible Intersectional Techno-Leadership” (RITL) playbook to govern these socio-technical complexities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Rather than a general literature review, this conceptual paper employs a targeted synthesis of recent discourse across twin transition dynamics, AI ethics, and strategic management. It integrates intersectionality theory into upper echelons logic to construct an actionable, context-aware leadership methodology suitable for diverse global environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis identifies a critical governance blind spot: the integration of digital and green strategies is not uniformly beneficial. Without intersectional oversight, AI tools can reproduce systemic historical inequalities, leading to what is formalized here as “algorithmic greenwashing.” The proposed RITL framework offers three operational levers for executives: Cognitive Audits (Strategic Awareness), Intersectional Talent Architecture (Structural Participation), and The Accountability Loop (Process Governance).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To address the operational ambiguity of the twin transition, the paper provides a highly specific, condition-aware “Monday Morning Checklist” for C-suite executives and policymakers. It offers concrete mechanisms to audit their AI supply chains and foster intersectional STEM ecosystems, ensuring that digital sustainability efforts mitigate, rather than exacerbate, corporate ESG risks across varying organizational contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Moving beyond the established consensus that digitalization and sustainability are linked, this paper contributes by problematizing the twin transition. It reframes intersectional inclusion not as a compliance cost, but as a strategic asset and risk-management firewall, offering a nuanced approach to AI governance that ensures sustainable futures are equitable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The AI-green paradox: mitigating algorithmic greenwashing through intersectional leadership in the twin transition

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Grounded in the Social Information Processing Theory (SIPT), the current study aims to examine the role of Diversity-focused HR Practices in promoting Inclusion Climate; simultaneously, it also investigates the role of Inclusive Leadership as a moderator in relationship explaining how it shapes inclusion at work.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional quantitative approach has been taken, and the survey data were collected from 232 professionals employed in Indian IT sector organizations. To perform the data analysis PLS-SEM was employed using SmartPLS4.1.0 software.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings reveal while diversity-focused HR practices contribute to fostering an inclusive climate, their impact depends significantly on leadership behavior. Inclusive leaders play a critical role in strengthening the effectiveness of these practices by shaping how employees experience inclusion in their teams.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings of the study imply the gravity that a leader holds in the workgroup. As exhibited by findings, leaders with their inclusive behavior act as a catalyst which transforms HR practices into an inclusive workplace. Therefore, investments in diversity policies must be accompanied by leadership development programs to convert formal initiatives into employees-lived workplace experience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study integrates HR practices and leadership perspectives by identifying inclusive leadership as a contextual boundary condition explaining variability in inclusion climate formation. This shifts scholarly attention from formal HR systems to the role of leaders as enablers of inclusion, demonstrating that leadership is a key mechanism through which diversity initiatives translate into meaningful workplace experiences, thereby providing a novel insight to the present literature.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Translating HR practices to inclusion climate: the moderating role of inclusive leadership

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on job demands–resources (JD-R) theory, this study examines how different leadership styles − transformational and authentic, shape workplace flourishing through the mediating role of trust within a highly disciplined and hierarchical military environment where discipline, resilience, and mission focus dominate organizing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Employing a quantitative research methodology, data for the inquiry from a survey of 292 military personnel, including commissioned and non-commissioned Officers based at a Military Hospital in Ghana. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was used to test the hypothesized relationships among leadership styles, trust, and workplace flourishing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study found a clear divergence in leadership effectiveness. Authentic leadership demonstrated a significant and positive direct influence on workplace flourishing, and trust partially mediated this relationship, indicating it is a key mechanism. Conversely, transformational leadership showed no significant direct or indirect effect on flourishing, with trust failing to act as a mediating variable. This analysis moves beyond stating what was found to explain the psychological and contextual reasons why: in the military’s rigid hierarchy, authentic leaders provide the psychological safety and demonstrable integrity needed to build trust, whereas transformational leaders’ inspirational rhetoric may be constrained by the chain of command and perceived as less genuine, thus failing to foster the deep trust required for holistic well-being. This suggests that in military contexts, where discipline, resilience, and mission focus dominate- authenticity and trust may play a more critical role than charisma or inspirational motivation in promoting well-being and performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings emphasize the need for military institutions to nurture leadership approaches that prioritize authenticity, ethical engagement, and transparent communication. Leadership development programs should integrate dedicated modules on authentic leadership to build trust and enhance personnel well-being, which is crucial for operational readiness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study challenges the assumed universal efficacy of transformational leadership by demonstrating that authentic leadership, via trust, is more effective in promoting flourishing within a disciplined military hierarchy, thereby identifying an important boundary condition for leadership theory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: How leadership fosters military flourishing: the critical role of trust

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Recent research has increasingly focused on the moral and ethical dimensions of leadership. This paper examines how the evolving concept of responsible leadership fosters employees’ trust within ethically fragile and institutionally unstable business environments. Rather than treating responsible leadership as a fixed normative framework, this study repositions it as a dynamic arena where diverse stakeholders hold conflicting expectations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study adopts an exploratory qualitative design, drawing on 22 in-depth semi-structured interviews within a case study framework. This methodology enabled a nuanced and thorough analysis of how employees perceive and navigate the complexities of trust dynamics in the organisational context.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Empirical evidence reveals diverse expectations of responsible leadership, shaped by multidimensional contextual factors such as religion and cultural norms. It argues that both relational and contextual factors illuminate the evolving processes through which leadership is legitimised, trust is sustained, and organisational cohesion is maintained amidst fragile formal systems and unstable societal institutions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While this paper broadens the concept of responsible leadership beyond a Western-centric perspective, its findings are largely drawn from a single organisational context. Given Nigeria’s considerable diversity, additional research is needed to strengthen these claims and improve the generalisability of the conclusions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper provides actionable insights for enhancing leadership and organisational development, especially in settings where institutional safeguards are fragile or uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By examining responsible leadership through the lens of the Nigerian context, this study underscores the role of local context in organisational research. Its findings emphasise the importance of developing leadership theories attuned to and adaptable to distinct cultural realities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Trust, religion and responsible leadership: how employees judge leaders in fragile institutional contexts

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This article introduces leadership dispensability capital as a capital-based way of assessing leadership-created organizational value. It argues that leadership should be judged not only by what a leader delivers while central, but also by what the organization retains when that centrality reduces. The article addresses a governance blind spot: organizations may praise indispensable leaders while accumulating dependency risk.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article is developed as a practitioner-facing conceptual framework paper. Drawing on leadership, governance, succession, distributed leadership, upper echelons, authority, knowledge management, and intellectual capital thinking, it defines Leadership Dispensability Capital as the organizational asset created when leadership transfers judgment, relationships, legitimacy, and execution capacity from person-bound advantage into system-bound capability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Concentrated leadership is not inherently problematic and may be necessary in early-stage, crisis, founder-led, or turnaround settings. The strategic risk appears when concentration continues after leader-held value should have been converted into wider organizational capability. Under those conditions, strong current performance may coexist with a dependency discount. Organizations that build Leadership Dispensability Capital may earn a replaceability premium because decision quality, stakeholder confidence, legitimacy, and execution reliability survive without recurring re-centralization around one person.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This conceptual article develops Leadership Dispensability Capital as a new construct rather than testing it empirically. Future research can operationalize the four dimensions, examine whether they develop together or unevenly, and test whether weak Leadership Dispensability Capital predicts transition disruption, stakeholder anxiety, strategic drift, or valuation concerns. Longitudinal studies could also examine when productive leader centrality becomes costly dependence, especially in founder-led firms, professional service organizations, family businesses, social enterprises, public agencies, and AI-enabled organizations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article gives boards and senior leaders a practical way to assess whether strong performance rests on retained organizational capability or continuing leader dependence. The proposed scorecard helps directors examine whether judgment, stakeholder trust, legitimacy, and execution quality can survive reduced leader centrality. It can be used in chief executive evaluation, succession planning, founder-scaling reviews, post-crisis reviews, and major growth transitions. The article also encourages leadership development to reward not only present performance, but also the leader’s ability to transfer, embed, and institutionalize value.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article highlights continuity risks in organizations that serve wider social purposes, including public, civic, educational, charitable, and community organizations. When trust, authority, purpose, and service quality rest too heavily on one individual, beneficiaries, employees, volunteers, donors, and communities may become exposed to avoidable disruption. Leadership Dispensability Capital encourages socially consequential organizations to build institutional trust, shared purpose, distributed legitimacy, and reproducible service quality so that essential work can continue even when a central leader steps back.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article makes three contributions. First, it introduces Leadership Dispensability Capital as a leadership-specific form of retained organizational value that connects leadership assessment with intellectual capital thinking. Second, it develops a capital-conversion model explaining how person-bound leadership value becomes system-bound capability. Third, it offers a board-facing scorecard for distinguishing healthy centrality from costly dependence before succession, crisis, growth, or AI-enabled acceleration exposes the weakness. Dispensability refers to reduced organizational dependence, not leader disposability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The replaceability premium: leadership dispensability capital and the hidden value of becoming less indispensable

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates the relationship between authentic leadership and employee work engagement, focusing on the mediating role of psychological empowerment among frontline employees in Ghana’s Food and Beverage (F&B) industry.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study adopted a descriptive time-lagged research design to capture temporal relationships among the variables. Data were collected from 315 non-managerial staff across 25 food and beverage establishments in Ghana at three separate intervals: authentic leadership at Time 1, psychological empowerment at Time 2, and employee work engagement at Time 3. Participants were selected using simple random sampling, and data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Both psychological empowerment and employee work engagement were modeled as reflective–formative second-order constructs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study found that authentic leadership positively and significantly relates to both psychological empowerment and employee work engagement. Also, the study’s findings revealed that psychological empowerment significantly and positively predicts employee work engagement. Further, psychological empowerment served as a partial mediator in the relationship between authentic leadership and employee work engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study advances leadership research by applying a reflective–formative second-order modeling approach to examine psychological empowerment as the mediating mechanism linking authentic leadership to employee work engagement in Ghana’s (F&B) sector—an underexplored context characterized by high-pressure service demands and resource constraints. It provides new insights into the mechanisms through which leadership style influences employee outcomes in frontline service environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Authentic leadership, psychological empowerment, and employee work engagement: a reflective-formative higher-order perspective

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purposes</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this study is to examine gender disparities in organizational leadership by analyzing fifteen years of U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data. Specifically, the study investigates trends in women’s workforce participation, their representation in senior roles—including Chief Executive positions—and the extent of gender gaps across occupations and industries.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study employs a longitudinal quantitative design using fifteen years of U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics time-series data. Gender representation in leadership and senior roles is assessed through percentage analysis and mean comparisons across occupations and industries. Group differences between men and women in senior positions and CEO roles are evaluated to determine the presence and magnitude of gender gaps.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis reveals persistent and substantial gender gaps in U.S. corporate leadership. Women remain significantly underrepresented in CEO and senior management roles across most occupations and industries, despite gradual increases in overall workforce participation. Sectors with traditionally high female representation show stronger leadership presence, while technical and engineering-related fields exhibit the widest disparities. Overall, women’s advancement to top leadership remains uneven and structurally constrained.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By identifying patterns in employment and leadership attainment, the study seeks to clarify whether a persistent gender gap exists and to deepen understanding of how gender influences access to senior organizational positions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This article offers a novel, data-driven assessment of gender disparities in U.S. corporate leadership by integrating sectoral, occupational, and hierarchical patterns into one analysis. Its value lies in translating statistical gaps into strategic implications for organizations, highlighting where structural barriers persist and why progress stalls. The study provides leaders with actionable insight into how gender representation shapes strategic capacity, culture, and long-term organizational performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Bridging the leadership divide: a longitudinal analysis of gender disparities in senior U.S. workforce roles

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This review examines whether rule based and technology enabled documentation controls are sufficient for public procurement integrity and identifies the governance capabilities that condition their effectiveness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following Okoli’s, 2015, eight stage guide and reporting against PRISMA 2020, EBSCO, ProQuest and Google Scholar were searched for English language, peer reviewed journal articles published between January 1, 2015 and March 4, 2026. Screening produced a 132 record analytic register, from which 48 studies were retrieved as archived full texts and appraised using design appropriate criteria informed by the Cochrane Handbook. Findings were organised into five conceptual themes and cross checked against seven evidence derived synthesis findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across the 48 studies, documentation rules, audit trails, e-procurement and open contracting platforms improved traceability and access, but their effects consistently depended on enforcement, capacity, leadership, ethical culture and meaningful stakeholder access rather than on adoption alone. No study demonstrated that formal or digital controls independently reduced corruption. The evidence supports complementarity between technical controls and governance capability, not the replacement of rules by leadership. The review formalises leadership mediated governance capability as a construct with three properties, develops a four layer documentation integrity framework, and advances four propositions specifying the conditions under which controls convert into substantive integrity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The English language and peer reviewed only criteria may have excluded relevant national language and institutional evidence, and the appraisal was not independently duplicated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The review reframes documentation integrity as an organisational and inter-organisational governance capability rather than an administrative compliance task, grounded in a quality appraised full text corpus and expressed in a testable propositional form.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Leadership mediated governance capability and procurement documentation integrity reform

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines the necessary conditions for Digital Strategic Renewal (DSR), testing whether digital leadership (DL), digital entrepreneurial orientation (DEO), strategic autonomy (SA), strategic ambidexterity (AMB), knowledge integration (KI), and governance support (GS) individually impose minimum floor constraints below which DSR cannot occur, regardless of other conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Necessary Condition Analysis was applied to a sample of 304 organizations actively pursuing digital transformation. Two ceiling estimators were used: CE-FDH as the primary estimator and CR-FDH as a robustness check. A bottleneck table was generated to identify minimum condition levels required at each DSR level.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four conditions are individually necessary for DSR: DEO (d = 0.298), GS (d = 0.281), AMB (d = 0.222), and DL (d = 0.196). SA is borderline necessary (CE-FDH: d = 0.137; CR-FDH: d = 0.096), with its ceiling effect concentrated at high DSR levels. KI does not impose an individual floor constraint (d = 0.081). A three-tier hierarchy of binding constraints emerges: DEO and AMB constrain outcomes at the lowest DSR levels; GS and DL become binding at moderate levels; SA becomes binding only at the most ambitious renewal levels a structural ordering rather than a temporal sequence, given the cross-sectional design. At the 80% DSR level, all five necessary conditions impose simultaneous active thresholds.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The cross-sectional design limits temporal inference about causal sequencing. The single-context sample constrains geographic generalizability. Future research should replicate the necessity envelope across institutional contexts with varying governance infrastructure and test the longitudinal stability of the escalating bottleneck structure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Organizations must clear a five-condition necessity floor appropriate to their targeted renewal ambition before pathway selection can be expected to translate into DSR outcomes. DEO and AMB constrain even low-ambition renewal; GS and DL become binding once ambition rises to moderate levels; SA is binding only at high ambition. Because these are floor conditions rather than success conditions, clearing them removes a structural barrier without guaranteeing renewal; a complementary sufficiency analysis is still required to identify which configurations actually produce high DSR. KI imposes no floor at low-to-moderate ambition but becomes a binding constraint once an organization targets the highest renewal tier, so it should not be treated as globally dispensable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study offers, to our knowledge, an initial application of standalone Necessary Condition Analysis to digital strategic renewal, identifying a five-condition necessity envelope and a tiered bottleneck structure that specifies which prerequisites bind at which levels of renewal ambition. This staged distinction between early-binding, moderate-binding, and high-DSR-only constraints complement existing variance-based and configurational findings by making explicit a structural feature of digital strategic renewal that sufficiency-oriented methods are not designed to detect. The primary contribution is methodological extending necessity logic to an established set of digital transformation constructs rather than the introduction of a new theoretical mechanism.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Necessary conditions for digital strategic renewal: a necessary condition analysis of digital leadership, entrepreneurial orientation, and governance support

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates whether self-leadership mediates the relationship between workforce agility and work performance among gig workers in India, a labour market projected to encompass 23.5 million platform workers by 2030.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A quantitative, cross-sectional design was employed. Data were collected from 248 active gig workers across India - spanning food delivery, ride-hailing, freelancing, home services, and e-commerce - using a structured 17-item, seven-point Likert scale questionnaire. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS 4, supplemented by SPSS 25, was used for analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Workforce agility significantly predicted self-leadership (ß = 0.594, p &lt; 0.001), and self-leadership significantly predicted work performance (ß = 0.565, p &lt; 0.001). The direct effect of workforce agility on work performance was non-significant (ß = 0.051, p = 0.402), while the indirect effect through self-leadership was significant (ß = 0.335, p &lt; 0.001), confirming full mediation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The cross-sectional design and purposive sampling limit causal inference and generalisability. Future research should employ longitudinal designs and objective platform performance data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Platform firms should invest in in-app goal-setting tools, performance dashboards, and self-leadership development modules. Policymakers should treat gig worker capability development as a productive economic investment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>With 23.5 million gig workers projected in India by 2030, cultivating self-leadership capacity carries significant implications for worker earnings, economic sustainability, and labour market equity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>

<jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Arts can be used in many different ways in leadership education. This paper explores how students perceive four different arts-based approaches: (1) design/ visual interpretation, (2) object construction, (3) practical theatre exercises, and (4) practical dance exercises.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Data were collected using a questionnaire distributed among students at a business school in Morocco. Students were asked about their perception of arts-based methods in leadership education and different learning objectives that can be achieved. The resulting dataset was subjected to a cluster analysis.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The analysis unveils four distinct patterns in which students respond to arts-based methods. For a majority of the students, arts-based methods are welcome, but there is also a small fraction of students who are consistently critical about them. Furthermore, the clusters allow distinctions between preferences for different arts and varying expectations regarding the learning objectives.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The study lays the groundwork for a typology of different target groups that need to be taken into account in planning the use of arts-based methods in class. It enables leadership education to apply such methods more effectively, respecting diverse preferences and abilities of learners when designing courses.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
title: Arts-based methods in leadership education – a cluster analysis from Northern Africa

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates the differential effects of transformational and authentic leadership on task performance within a high-stakes organizational context. It specifically examines the mediating roles of trust in leadership and psychological safety in these relationships.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A mixed-methods explanatory sequential design was employed, grounded in Social Exchange Theory and the Job Demands-Resources model. Quantitative data were collected from 292 military personnel in the Ghana Armed Forces using validated questionnaires and analyzed via Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). Qualitative insights from 18 semi-structured interviews provided contextual depth to the findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings reveal a critical distinction within this specific context: while both leadership styles positively influence task performance, they operate through fundamentally different mechanisms. Authentic leadership appears to enhance task performance both directly and indirectly, through the partial mediation of trust and psychological safety. In contrast, transformational leadership’s influence on performance is fully mediated by psychological safety, with trust playing no mediating role. These findings suggest that, in hierarchical, high-stress military environments, authentic leadership appears to be more effective in building the relational resources (trust) necessary for sustained performance. However, given the cross-sectional design and single-country, single-organizational context, these findings require replication and should be interpreted with appropriate caution.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study challenges the universal applicability of transformational leadership theory and extends the Job Demands-Resources model by demonstrating that leadership behaviors function as differentiated job resources with style-specific pathways to performance. These findings provide robust evidence for HRM practitioners and policymakers to prioritize the development of authentic, transparent and ethical leadership to foster a high-performing and psychologically healthy workforce.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Transformational vs. authentic leadership in task performance: the mediating roles of trust and psychological safety

<jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study investigates the impacts of transformational, transactional, and authoritarian leadership styles on employees’ strategic thinking and examines whether leader gender moderates these relationships.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Drawing on empirical data from 203 employees from a higher education institution in Ghana, data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and the statistical package for the social sciences (SPSS).</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The results indicated that transformational leadership has a significant positive effect on employees’ strategic thinking. In contrast, transactional and authoritarian leadership styles showed no significant effect. Additionally, leader gender did not moderate the relationship between leadership styles and employees’ strategic thinking.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The cross-sectional nature of the study limits the ability to draw causal inferences and may not capture the dynamic nature of leadership interactions over time, limiting the ability to generalize the findings.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The findings emphasize the importance of transformational leadership in promoting strategic thinking among employees. Institutional leaders are encouraged to adopt transformational behaviors to enhance strategic thinking skills.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Higher education institutions must create an inclusive and innovative culture that empowers marginalized groups to participate in strategic decision-making toward broader societal progress.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study makes a significant contribution to the leadership literature by investigating the often-overlooked moderating influence of gender on the relationship between leadership styles and strategic thinking. Studies using SET to explain gender, strategic thinking, and leadership within higher education settings in Ghana are woefully inadequate.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
title: Leadership styles and employees’ strategic thinking: does leader gender moderate these relationships?

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this paper is to examine when AI-assisted compassion signalling preserves credibility during consequential organisational change and when it instead weakens execution. Organisations increasingly have to communicate care while implementing change that imposes visible loss. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) makes compassion language fast, plentiful and inexpensive to produce.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This is a conceptual theory-building paper. It uses two illustrative vignettes to surface the phenomenon, integrates compassion research, signalling theory, strategic leadership, emotional labour, symbolic management, trust repair and human–AI communication, defines Synthetic Compassion as a distinct construct, develops a recipient inference mechanism, and derives propositions, a leadership playbook, governance requirements and a staged empirical pathway with illustrative measures.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Warm language is no longer sufficiently diagnostic once its production cost collapses. Synthetic Compassion supports cooperation when recipients can identify a named human owner, understand the process that follows the message, and expect workable recourse within a credible time frame. It backfires when delegation cues lower effort inference, blur ownership or reveal a remedy system that cannot absorb the volume created by scaled messaging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper is conceptual and does not claim empirical validation. The vignettes are analytic illustrations rather than data. The manuscript therefore prioritises testable propositions, illustrative operationalisations, and a staged research agenda spanning vignette experiments, field audits and longitudinal designs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper offers a streamlined leadership playbook consisting of a pre-release diagnostic, a three-state readiness screen, a stepwise implementation sequence, illustrative deployment heuristics for scale and recourse, and post-deployment monitoring indicators. It also specifies a rapid-cycle minimum bundle for crisis or time-compressed settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Better governance of AI-mediated care communication can reduce cynicism, preserve trust in institutions, and improve how employees, citizens, patients and service users experience disruptive change.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper introduces Synthetic Compassion as a bounded strategic leadership construct rather than a relabelling of generic impression management, organisational hypocrisy or broad AI trust. Its distinctive contribution is to explain an earlier-stage credibility mechanism: recipients may discount compassion language before the full action record is visible because scalable language shifts interpretive weight from warmth to ownership, procedural legibility and remedy capacity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Synthetic compassion: when GenAI scales care language and makes credibility the binding constraint in strategic leadership

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study tests whether digital readiness depends on the strategic fit between transformational leadership and digital infrastructure in micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs). Rather than treating infrastructure as a mediator of leadership, this study examines whether leadership and infrastructure must be aligned and jointly strong for readiness to emerge.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were collected between August and October 2024. The retained analytical file contained 500 de-identified questionnaire records and nine study indicators. Three equal-weighted component indices were constructed. Leadership and infrastructure were centered on the common value of 4.0 to preserve their substantive equality line, after which polynomial regression and response surface analysis (RSA) were estimated using HC3 heteroscedasticity-consistent inference.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The data do not support the expected strategic fit explanation. The polynomial model explained 1.0% of the variance in digital readiness (R2 = 0.010; adjusted R2 = −0.0001; robust F(5, 494) = 0.959, p = 0.442). The leadership × infrastructure term was not significant (b = −0.107, p = 0.311), and neither the line-of-congruence slope (a1 = −0.062, p = 0.283) nor the line-of-incongruence curvature (a4 = 0.086, p = 0.639) was significant. Thus, high leadership-infrastructure alignment was not associated with higher readiness in the retained analytical file.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study shifts the debate from mediation to strategic fit. Its null result places an empirical boundary on the common assumption that visionary leadership and digital infrastructure automatically reinforce one another. For resource-constrained MSMEs, alignment between managerial intent and technology possession may be insufficient unless additional integrating mechanisms—such as digital routines, employee capability, governance, and actual technology use—are in place.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Does leadership–infrastructure fit explain digital readiness?

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The present research investigates the role of Green Humble Leadership (GHL) in Green Creativity (GC) in the hotel industry. The study combines both the Social Exchange Theory (SET) and the Conservation of Resources Theory (COR) to comprehend the role of Green Humble Leadership (GHL) in developing creative and sustainable solutions within an environment that is eco-oriented.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study analyses data of 274 employees of a hotel in Swat region of Pakistan in a moderated-mediation model. Green Work Engagement (GWE) is viewed as a mediator whereas Perceived Organizational Support (POS) is viewed as a moderator in the relationship between Green Humble Leadership (GHL) and Green Creativity (GC).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicate that Green Humble Leadership (GHL) also has a considerable effect on Green Work Engagement (GWE) and Green Creativity (GC). Nevertheless, overindulgence in green work can cause depletion of resources, and this will diminish resourcefulness. The Perceived Organizational Support (POS) increases the impact of Green Humble Leadership (GHL) on Green Creativity (GC) by increasing the role of Green Work Engagement (GWE), meaning the relevance of supportive organizational structures.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research paper underlines the two fold functions of Green Humble Leadership (GHL) as a factor that contributes to Green Creativity (GC) green creativity, and it also indicates the limitations that may be brought about by overworking. It proposes that companies encourage the eco-innovation through balancing leadership practices with sufficient support systems that will guarantee continued creativity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study supplements the existing body of knowledge on leadership by showing the multi-faceted interaction between leadership, engagement and creativity in sustainable hospitality. It contributes to the green leadership discourse by suggesting a new emphasis from transformational or empowering styles to a humility-based approach. In addition, it addresses the previously unexplored paradox of overworking while engaged in eco-innovative activities, but considering a developing country in terms of tourism.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Harnessing green humble leadership to foster green creativity through moderated-mediation model

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) will transform various processes by utilizing and sharing data and information. This transformation brings new opportunities and challenges to organizations. Effective leadership is essential to handle these changes. However, there is no scientific research on how AI affects the everyday lives of managers. Therefore, this paper aims to identify how AI can affect changes in the skills and personality traits of managers using AI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A structured literature review identified leadership competencies relevant to the AI era. Three scientific databases were included in the search: (I) Scopus, (II) EBSCO Business Source Complete, and (III) Web of Science. A total of 730 articles were identified from the three databases under the topics “Digital Leadership,” “Leadership” AND “Artificial Intelligence,” “Future Leadership,” “Algorithm Leadership,” “AI Leadership,” “Artificial Leadership,” and “Data-driven Leadership.”</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 24 leadership competencies, including 12 personality traits and 12 skills, were identified from the literature. To adapt effectively to AI, leaders should focus on developing communication skills and forming high-performance teams working cross-functionally and in a symbiosis of humans and machines.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article adds knowledge to leadership theories and provides a basis for future management education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Leadership-competences in the era of artificial intelligence – a structured review

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This conceptual article examines how military principles of mission command can be translated to civilian leadership contexts, and how these principles conceptualize intention-based leadership and structured flexibility as a response to VUCA conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Through comparative analysis of six Western military doctrines and a narrative review of contemporary leadership theory, the study develops intention-based leadership as a civilian framework grounded in military mission command principles.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis reveals three conceptual contributions. First, intention-based leadership specifies intent as the active coordination mechanism, not trust alone, but articulated purpose, boundaries, priorities, decision rights, and success criteria. Second, normal accountability is preserved through intent alignment as the evaluative basis, shifting assessment from plan compliance to judgment quality. Third, a dual architecture of centralized strategic intent with decentralized tactical execution operationalizes structured flexibility as a hybrid model bridging heroic and post-heroic paradigms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article addresses what Schweiger et al. (2020) identify as a persistent gap; a processual approach to leadership that maintains necessary accountability structures. By specifying the coordination mechanism, accountability basis, and architectural logic of structured flexibility, the framework provides conceptual clarity for implementing post-heroic leadership within formal organizations. A set of propositions are developed for further empirical investigation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Structured flexibility in VUCA environments: conceptualizing intention-based leadership through military mission command principles

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how leadership justice relates to innovative work behavior among R&D employees in China’s new energy vehicle (NEV) industry, contributing to climate action, with a focus craftsman spirit and job embeddedness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were collected from 200 R&D employees in listed NEV firms in Jiangsu province. SmartPLS (PLS-SEM) was used to assess the measurement model and test direct, mediating and moderating effects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Leadership justice is positively associated with leader trust, which, in turn, is linked to stronger craftsman spirit and higher innovative work behavior. Craftsman spirit mediates the relationship between leader trust and innovative work behavior. Job embeddedness does not significantly moderate the relationship between leader trust and craftsman spirit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The cross-sectional, single-province design limits causal inference and generalizability. Future work should use longitudinal, multi-source data and test alternative moderators in the NEV context.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Managers can promote innovative work behavior by institutionalizing fairness, transparency and craftsmanship standards. Job embeddedness may aid retention but may not strengthen innovation pathways.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The cross-sectional, single-province design limits causal inference and generalizability. Future work should use longitudinal, multi-source data and test alternative moderators in the NEV context.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Leadership justice and innovative work behaviour: the roles of leader trust, craftsman spirit, and job embeddedness

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study focuses on the influence of digital transformation and responsible leadership on green innovation by examining the mediating role of knowledge sharing and the moderating role of organizational culture in SMEs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 379 responses were collected using a questionnaire survey from hierarchical levels of SMEs employees, and the PROCESS application was employed to evaluate the hypothesized relationships.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Results indicate that knowledge sharing partially mediates the influence of digital transformation and responsible leadership on green innovation in SMEs. Furthermore, organizational culture does not moderate the influence of knowledge sharing on green innovation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study offers valuable insights for managers to enhance the values of digital transformation and responsible leadership in SMEs to promote green innovation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research contributes to existing literature by consolidating digital transformation and responsible leadership to create green innovation in SMEs with the efficacy of resource-based view (RBV) – thereby contributing to a novel area of SMEs literature.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Examining how digital transformation and responsible leadership affect green innovation in SMEs: a moderated and mediation model

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Over the past two decades, the issue of environmental concerns has garnered growing global attention. The primary objective of this study is to investigate the relationship between green transformational leadership and firm performance, with two mediating variables, environmental passion and environmental strategies, as well as control variables. This paper offers critical new insights into how ecological passion, combined with Green Transformational Leadership, enhances corporate performance through environmental strategy. The role of green transformational leadership is to improve firm performance and motivate both the leader and others toward a sustainable environment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We obtained data from 1512 respondents working in SME manufacturing companies in China, using a convenience sample approach. The two software packages used in this study are Smart PLS, R, and SPSS for data analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our findings, based on the data, indicate that the role of green transformational leadership in firm performance is significant, with the two mediating variables of environmental passion and environmental strategies also contributing to firm performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides a novel contribution by empirically linking green leadership to firm performance through dual mediators, environmental passion and strategy. It highlights the psychological and strategic mechanisms through which sustainable leadership translates into measurable organizational benefits, offering practical implications for business leaders and policymakers focused on sustainability and performance enhancement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Green transformational leadership and firm performance: the mediating role of environmental passion and strategies

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study addresses gaps in leadership research concerning inconsistent empirical evidence on gender differences in leadership styles (LS), limited understanding of leadership practices in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), and insufficient cross-cultural comparison with Anglo leadership contexts. It examines whether gender differences in LS vary in Anglo and SSA cultural clusters, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of leadership in culturally diverse settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Leaders completed a self-administered Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire (MLQ) to measure transformational leadership style (TFLS), transactional leadership style (TALS) and laissez-faire leadership style (LFLS). The sample comprised leaders undertaking Master of Business Administration (MBA) programmes across Anglo and SSA clusters. Data were analysed using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS), applying univariate, bivariate, and multivariate statistical techniques to examine the effects of gender and culture on LS.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicate that men in both Anglo and SSA cultural clusters reported a higher transformational leadership score than women. No significant differences were found between native-born and resident leaders. Moderation analyses indicated that gender remained a significant predictor of transformational leadership, whereas no significant moderation effect of cultural context was identified. These findings suggest that gender differences in transformational leadership were relatively consistent across the examined cultural contexts. However, conclusions regarding moderation effects for transactional and laissez-faire leadership should be interpreted cautiously, as the statistical power of these models was limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study is limited by its reliance on a sample of professionally educated leaders, which may restrict generalisability to leaders without formal leadership education. Future research should examine additional leadership styles and assess the reliability of specific MLQ dimensions. Longitudinal and more diverse samples would further enhance understanding of how gender and cultural expectations interact to shape leadership behaviour.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The absence of a significant moderating effect of cultural context suggests that organisations should avoid assuming that leadership behaviours associated with gender necessarily differ across cultural settings. Leadership recruitment, promotion, and development should therefore focus primarily on demonstrated leadership competencies rather than demographic assumptions. Structured behavioural interviews, competency-based assessments, and leadership simulations can provide more objective evaluations of leadership capability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As organisations increasingly operate across national boundaries, leaders are required to work effectively with culturally diverse teams. A more nuanced understanding of leadership perceptions may contribute to fairer evaluations of individuals, stronger cross-cultural communication and collaboration and support effective leadership across international teams.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The first integration of Global Leadership and Organizational Behavior Effectiveness (GLOBE) cultural clusters with MLQ self-report data at the individual leader level in an Anglo-SSA comparison provides a more nuanced examination of the relationship between gender, cultural context, and leadership styles.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Do gender and culture shape leadership styles? Evidence from Anglo and Sub-Saharan African managers

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to examine how green human resource management influences low-carbon behavior and sustainable performance, while assessing the moderating and moderated mediation role of sustainable leadership within the context of Vietnam’s steel industry.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A quantitative approach was employed using survey data collected from 260 employees, managers and business owners in steel enterprises in Vietnam. Stratified sampling was applied, and hypotheses were tested using partial least squares structural equation modelling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicate that green human resource management significantly promotes employees’ low-carbon behavior but does not directly improve sustainable performance. Low carbon behavior fully mediates the relationship between green human resource management and sustainable performance. In addition, sustainable leadership strengthens the relationship between green human resource management and low-carbon behavior and exerts a significant moderated mediation effect on the indirect relationship between green human resource management and sustainable performance through low-carbon behavior.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to the literature by integrating ability motivation opportunity theory and social cognitive theory to explain the mechanism linking green human resource management, employee behavior and sustainable performance. It also provides empirical evidence from a high emission industry in an emerging economy, highlighting the critical role of leadership in translating green practices into sustainable outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Unlocking low-carbon behavior through green human resource management: the moderated mediation role of sustainable leadership

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study, employing ambidexterity theory, resource-based view (RBV) theory, and dynamic capabilities perspective, aims to investigate the impact of green ambidextrous leadership (GAL) on sustainability performance in ISO 14001-certified manufacturing companies in Malaysia. This adoption is viewed as a crucial step towards achieving green innovation initiatives (GII) and sustainable performance (SP) in ISO 14001-certified manufacturing companies in Malaysia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The research employed a quantitative research design, with the population comprising 488 owner-managers of ISO 14001-certified manufacturing companies in Malaysia. This study adopted a multistage sampling technique and analyzed 287 questionnaires. Using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling, exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, path analysis, and mediation and moderation analysis were conducted on the data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study demonstrates that green ambidextrous leadership can significantly enhance SP, a crucial finding for current ISO-14001 certified manufacturing companies in Malaysia. This research explores governance ambidexterity as a boundary condition for this relationship. Additionally, this study contributes to the literature on green strategies in ISO 14001-certified manufacturing companies in Malaysia by providing practical significance to policymakers who wish to implement green strategies to enhance overall sustainable performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study is limited to Malaysian manufacturing companies that are ISO 14001 certified, with data collected from a cross-sectional design and a sample size of 488 firms obtained solely from the FMM Directory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings suggest that Malaysian ISO 14001-certified manufacturing companies should invest in the enhancement of green ambidextrous leadership to reinforce green innovation initiatives that can be practically implemented and be consistent with the sustainability goals. Investing in leadership skills that create a balance between environmental exploration and operational exploitation, companies can maximize the effectiveness of green innovation processes and can increase sustainability performance beyond compliance-driven practices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study outlines a clear and actionable pathway for ISO-14001-certified manufacturing companies in Malaysia to achieve sector sustainability ( Economic, social and environment) performance, thereby enlightening the reader on the potential of GAL and GII in ISO-14001-certified manufacturing companies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three major contributions are provided through this study. First, it combines the ambidexterity and resource-based view theory with the dynamic capabilities perspective in pointing out how the green innovation initiatives mediate the association between green ambidextrous leadership and sustainability performance and governance ambidexterity as a boundary condition. Second, it offers empirical findings regarding manufacturers (certified according to ISO 14001) in Malaysia, which is an under-researched but policy-sensitive setting. Third, the study contributes to the research by describing a leadership-innovation-governance route where certified manufacturers can better transform environmental initiatives into sustainability performance outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Green ambidextrous leadership and green innovation initiatives as drivers of sustainability performance: evidence from ISO14001-certified manufacturing firms in Malaysia

<jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study aims to explore the impact of occupational stress (OS) on the innovative entrepreneurial capabilities (IEC) and innovative work behavior (IWB) of female entrepreneurs operating in dissimilar economies. Canada, an advanced economy, and Pakistan, an emerging economy, provided contrasting economic backgrounds for the investigation.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Data collected from 106 female entrepreneurs (53 each from Canada and Pakistan) were quantitatively analyzed through partial least squares structural equation modeling. In addition, funnel approach (a secondary technique) was used to understand the in-depth trends and variation among contrasting economies.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The results from this study show that IEC and IWB are statistically significantly affected by OS (IEC = 0.001 &lt; 0.05; p &lt; α; IWB = 0.000 &lt; 0.05; p &lt; α). The causes of stress for Pakistani female entrepreneurs are commonly personal factors, while organizational factors affected Canadian female entrepreneurs frequently. Consequences of stress relating to behavioral and physical deterioration are evident among Pakistani female entrepreneurs, while emotional symptoms are evident among Canadian female entrepreneurs.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Female entrepreneurs need to understand the relationship between their economic background and the likely impact of OS on their IEC and IWB. Furthermore, appropriate measures suited to economic context are required in managing the effect of OS by female entrepreneurs.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
               <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study contributes to the literature on entrepreneurship and effective leadership by highlighting the occupational stressors that affect female entrepreneurs operating in contrasting economies and the impact of these stressors on their IEC and IWB.</jats:p>
               </jats:sec>
title: The stress-innovation link: leadership and strategies of female entrepreneurs in diverse economies
