<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines the dual nature of charismatic and value-driven leadership in contemporary public contexts, where deep loyalty and unity can enhance strategic execution but also heighten conformity and reduce adaptability. It investigates how cultic influence patterns-such as charisma, dependency, identification, boundary control, and spiritual messaging-shape group cohesion and behavioral conformity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A quantitative, cross-sectional design was employed to test a mediation model linking leadership influence patterns to behavioral conformity through group cohesion. Data were collected from 456 participants involved in spiritual or quasi-spiritual leadership contexts. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was used to test direct and indirect effects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Charismatic authority, follower dependency, leader–follower identification, and spiritual messaging intensity all significantly enhanced group cohesion, with spiritual messaging emerging as the strongest predictor. Group cohesion, in turn, fully mediated the effects of leadership traits on behavioral conformity. Social isolation tactics were non-significant, challenging assumptions about boundary control as a unifying strategy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results provide guidance for leaders and policymakers on fostering cohesion without promoting uncritical conformity. Cultivating openness to dissent and ethical reflection can sustain unity while preserving adaptability, innovation, and responsible governance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study reframes cultic influence as a continuum of leadership practices with both strategic value and potential risk. By integrating psychological, relational, and spiritual communication perspectives, it offers a unified framework for understanding how moral authority and cohesion shape collective behavior in complex public leadership environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Cultic influence in public leadership: balancing cohesion, conformity, and strategic adaptability

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mining is a high environmental impact activity, yet it holds a high economic value to an economy. The motivation of this paper is to theorize Leadership as the prime antecedent in balancing the economic benefits of mining with environmental sustainability. The study, therefore, theorizes that green leadership is an antecedent to green innovation among mining firms within an enabling, green, entrepreneurial-oriented firm strategy. Integrating the transformational leadership theory and the resource-based view of the firm, the study investigates the mechanisms through which leadership fosters sustainable innovation in the mining sector.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A quantitative research design was employed using a structured questionnaire administered to 355 employees of mining firms in Obuasi, Ghana. Participants were selected based on experience, leadership exposure and engagement in environmental projects. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to test hypothesized relationships, supported by bootstrapping techniques.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicate that green leadership significantly influences both Green Entrepreneurial orientation (GEO) and Green Innovation (GI). Furthermore, GEO positively impacts GI and significantly mediates the relationship between Green Leadership (GL) and GI. However, the study finds no significant moderating effect of GEO on the GL–GI relationship. These findings underscore the importance of fostering entrepreneurial orientation as a conduit through which green leadership translates into innovative environmental practices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to the growing literature on sustainable organizational practices by offering new empirical insights from the under-researched mining sector of a developing economy. By establishing the mediating role of GEO and refuting its moderating role, the research provides a nuanced understanding of how leadership and entrepreneurial orientation interact to promote innovation. The findings have practical implications for policy and organizational strategy, particularly in high-impact industries grappling with environmental sustainability problems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The role of green entrepreneurial orientation in green leadership and green innovation: a moderated mediation analysis

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Focused on Indonesia’s manufacturing sector, where SMEs dominate and environmental regulations evolve. This study examines how ambidextrous leadership drives sustainability performance through green innovation, addressing a critical gap in emerging economies. By integrating the Natural Resource-Based View, we reveal how leaders’ dual exploration-exploitation capabilities foster green product and process innovation, transforming environmental challenges into competitive advantages.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a robust quantitative analysis of 392 Indonesian manufacturing leaders, we demonstrate that ambidextrous leadership not only directly enhances sustainability performance (ß = 0.43, p &lt; 0.001) but also indirectly through green product innovation (ß = 0.26, p &lt; 0.001). Notably, green product innovation outperforms process innovation in this context, likely due to Indonesia’s growing consumer demand for eco-friendly goods.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings offer actionable insights for policymakers and business leaders, showing that targeted leadership training and green R&D incentives can accelerate progress toward Indonesia’s 2060 net-zero agenda. This study advances leadership theory by contextualizing ambidexterity in resource-constrained settings and redefining sustainability pathways for developing nations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study breaks new ground by integrating the Natural Resource-Based View with ambidextrous leadership theory, revealing how leaders in Indonesia’s manufacturing sector leverage green innovation to achieve sustainability. Unlike prior research focused on Western contexts, we uncover the critical mediating roles of green product and process innovation in an emerging economy, where SME dynamics and regulatory pressures shape outcomes. The findings offer a novel framework for policymakers, linking leadership training to Indonesia’s 2060 net-zero targets. This research redefines sustainability leadership in resource-constrained settings, providing actionable strategies for balancing exploration and exploitation in green transitions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Ambidextrous leadership and sustainability performance: the mediating role of green product innovation and green process innovation

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this paper is to explore the effect of Entrepreneurial Leadership (EL) on Innovation Performance (IP) with the mediation of Organizational Learning Culture (OLC) and the moderation of Artificial Intelligence Adoption (AIA). There is little empirical evidence encompassing the complex elements of EL and OLC in the context of Indian companies. The authors believe that this study can support leaders in implementing the right strategies to foster a learning culture and drive innovation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An empirical study of 241 employees working in entrepreneurial ventures across India was conducted using a survey questionnaire. Structural Equation Modeling was used to examine the mediation and moderation effects using the SPSS AMOS statistical package.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings of this study align with existing research in that EL does affect the OLC, and AIA plays a moderator role in this effect. However, OLC is not found to affect IP. The authors suggest that future researchers in this field can take into account other organizational features to examine the effect more closely.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study’s findings are limited by contextual factors and sample demographics. Future research should explore additional organizational traits and technological readiness for a deeper understanding of innovation performance enablers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings of this study can be useful for practitioners, i.e. entrepreneurial leaders, in implementing strategies to drive a continuous learning and innovation culture throughout the firm to mitigate the effects of dynamism in external business environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Entrepreneurial leadership, AI adoption, and innovation performance: evidence from Indian entrepreneurial ventures

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Organizations seek leaders capable of providing competitive advantages in complex markets; however, recruiting leaders can be quite challenging, given that it is unclear which psychosocial characteristics are considered relevant. This study identifies the psychosocial skills and characteristics considered important in the recruitment and selection of persons for leadership positions in any given organizational context.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The protocol has been registered in the Open Science Framework (OSF) database and has followed the PRISMA model. The analysis included seven databases. The JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist was used to analyze the methodological quality of the included studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The systematic review results identified four articles that met the inclusion criteria, revealing nine relevant psychosocial skills and characteristics in the leaders’ recruitment process.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Future research should continue to develop knowledge on this domain because the actual amount of studies are quite insufficient to provide clear guidelines about how leaders are recruited and selected for distinct organizations and contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This is one of first systematic review analyzing psychosocial characteristics considered important in the recruitment and selection of persons for leadership positions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Review of recruitment and selection for leadership positions: evidence from a systematic review

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research addresses the escalating scholar-practitioner divide by investigating the conceptual divergence between academic leadership theory and dominant leadership discourse consumed and operationalized by practitioners. It seeks to synthesize fragmented perspectives into a coherent framework, identifying emergent imperatives and theoretical empty spaces necessitated by global organizational volatility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study employs a bifurcated methodological design. First, an inductive thematic analysis was carried out on executive-led discourse from select high-salience platforms. Second, a systematic morphological analysis mapped the current academic landscape. The findings of these studies were integrated via a cross-consistency assessment to bring together these disparate epistemological domains.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study utilized an inductive thematic analysis that crystallized six core themes, outlining the current ontological shift in leadership discourse. Through the General Morphological Analysis (GMA) the mapping of a multi-dimensional configuration space, identifying 165 structural research gaps in academic inquiry. These distinct epistemological domains were integrated, culminating in a 2x2 analytical quadrant that effectively triangulates conversational salience with theoretical density which provides a predictive roadmap for high-impact, ecologically valid inquiry by demarcating research voids and scholarly foundations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study is limited by the temporal snapshot of digital discourse and the inherent subjectivity of morphological parameterization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study seeks to bridge the scholar-practitioner divide through bringing together topics of both temporal and research interest toward actionable strategic imperatives. These imperatives facilitate the immediate operationalization of constructs such as ontological self-development, social architecture and the human-technology counterbalance to transition from traditional command structures toward decentralized, adaptive leadership paradigms essential for contemporary high-volatility environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study highlights a vital shift toward follower-centricity, ensuring that leadership transcends traditional power hierarchies to prioritize the well-being of the collective. These insights foster more resilient social structures capable of navigating the profound uncertainties of contemporary global disruption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Unlike previous literature which treats the scholar-practitioner divide as a monolithic challenge, this study, via thematic analysis and General Morphological Analysis provides a granular, empirical mapping of the current leadership topography. By delineating three distinct archetypal zones and synthesizing them into an analytical matrix to offer a predictive roadmap ensuring that future scholarly inquiry is both theoretically rigorous and ecologically valid.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Bridging the scholar-practitioner divide: analysis of emerging leadership imperatives in academic inquiry & corporate discourse

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how organizational culture support influences sustainability ambidexterity, focusing on the mediating roles of business model transformation and firm identity coherence, as well as the moderating role of leadership orientation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on organizational identity theory, the study uses survey data from 350 firms in Ghana and applies PLS-SEM analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings show that supportive organizational cultures significantly enhance firms’ ability to balance exploratory and exploitative sustainability practices. This relationship functions via structural transformation and identity alignment mechanisms. However, leadership orientation weakens the positive influence of culture on sustainability ambidexterity, suggesting that overly directive leadership may constrain adaptive learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings suggest that managers should foster a supportive and adaptive organizational culture to enhance sustainability ambidexterity while carefully aligning leadership orientation to avoid undermining the positive effects of cultural support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study contributes to the sustainability management literature by integrating cultural, strategic and identity perspectives and offers actionable insights for managers seeking to foster sustainable organizational capabilities. This study uniquely demonstrates that sustainability ambidexterity is driven by parallel structural and cognitive mechanisms rather than sequential processes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Organisational culture support and sustainability ambidexterity: the roles of leadership orientation and firm identity coherence

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to investigate the influence of transformational leadership (TL) on product and process innovation in the banking sector, emphasizing the moderating role of knowledge sharing (KS). While TL has been recognized for fostering innovation through mechanisms such as idealized influence, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration, its interplay with KS remains underexplored in the context of developing economies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was adopted. Data were collected from 418 employees working in banks in Jordan, using self-administered in person survey. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was employed to test the hypotheses and validate the proposed conceptual framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings affirm a direct positive relationship between TL and both product and process innovation. Moreover, KS showed a moderation effect on the relation between TL on one side and both process and product innovation on the other. The impact of TL on the ProdInn and ProcInn was strengthened with the moderation of KS among employees with banking sector.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study provides valuable insights for both theory and practice, recommending enhanced TL practices and organizational strategies to foster innovation, including building trust and encouraging knowledge-sharing behaviors. Future research should explore these dynamics across diverse sectors and longitudinal contexts to deepen understanding of TL’s role in driving innovation. Practically, the findings underscore crucial considerations for banking sector aiming to effectively leverage TL to improve process and product innovation that will lead to improved performance and competitive advantage.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Driving innovation in banking sector: the role of transformational leadership and knowledge sharing

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates how digital transformational leadership moderates and digital knowledge acquisition mediates the relationship between digital platform capability and sustainable competitive advantage in emerging market manufacturing SMEs. It theoretically extends dynamic capabilities and practically guides resource-constrained firms in digitalization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The authors collected data from 385 manufacturing SMEs in an emerging market using a time-lagged research design. A research model was developed to test the proposed relationships through quantitative analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The empirical results show that digital platform capability positively affects sustainable competitive advantage through digital knowledge acquisition as a critical mediating mechanism. Furthermore, digital transformational leadership significantly moderates both the relationship between digital platform capability and knowledge acquisition and the overall mediation pathway.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study suggests that manufacturing SMEs should develop digital platform capabilities alongside digital transformational leadership to achieve sustainable competitive advantage. Managers and policy-makers must prioritize leadership training and digital infrastructure to overcome environmental volatility. Moreover, leveraging digital knowledge acquisition as a mediating mechanism can enhance innovation performance and competitive positioning in digitalized business landscapes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to the literature by elucidating how leadership approaches can maximize digital capabilities in resource-constrained environments. Additionally, by revealing the mediating role of knowledge acquisition and the moderating effects of transformational leadership, this study enriches the research on dynamic capabilities theory in the context of digital transformation in emerging markets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Leadership and digital platforms: building sustainable advantage in emerging markets

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to map the intellectual structure, thematic evolution and research agenda of leadership as organizational intellectual capital through bibliometric analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The authors analyzed 439 English-language Web of Science Core Collection publications through 31 December 2025. Performance analysis, bibliographic coupling and co-word analysis in VOSviewer identified influential publications, thematic clusters and emerging trajectories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The field has progressed from treating leadership and intellectual capital separately to an integrated domain centered on innovation, sustainability, knowledge management and resilience. Five bibliographic coupling streams address intellectual capital utilization, governance, knowledge strategy, value creation and entrepreneurial transformation. Co-word analysis highlights sustainability, dynamic capabilities, social capital, creativity and leadership-driven intellectual-capital systems, positioning leadership as an architect of sustainable value creation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study reconceptualizes leadership as dynamic, systemic organizational capital and provides a current synthesis and research agenda for leadership and intellectual-capital scholarship.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The contested relationship between leadership and intellectual capital: a review and research agenda

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite sustained investment in gender diversity initiatives, women remain significantly underrepresented in senior leadership roles across many industries. This study aims to examine why increased recruitment and mentoring initiatives often fail to translate into leadership advancement for women in India’s automotive manufacturing sector, one of the country’s most engineering-intensive and male-dominated blue collared industries. The study explores whether authentic leadership can function as a strategic organisational capability that strengthens leadership pipelines and facilitates women’s advancement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study draws on qualitative evidence from 25 women occupying mid to senior to executive level and five focus groups conducted across major Indian automotive firms. Data were analysed using thematic analysis. This approach included familiarisation with the data, systematic coding, theme development, refinement and synthesising resulting in patterns across participants experiences while maintaining sensitivity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings identify a consistent progression in leadership advancement. Authentic leadership strengthens trust; trust enables sponsorship; and sponsorship drives leadership mobility. While organisations frequently invest in mentoring and diversity hiring targets, structured sponsorship mechanisms that translate credibility into advancement opportunities remain largely absent. This absence contributes to leadership pipelines that stagnate at mid-management levels.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study introduces the strategic engine of leadership equity framework, which positions authentic leadership as a system-level capability rather than an individual leadership trait. Five organisational levers are proposed to embed authenticity within leadership development systems, performance evaluation structures, sponsorship pathways, organisational culture and leadership accountability mechanisms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By examining women’s leadership advancement in India’s automotive manufacturing sector, the study extends leadership scholarship beyond Western service-sector contexts. It provides a practical strategic framework for organisations seeking to convert diversity intentions into measurable leadership progression in male-dominated blue-collar industries.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Authentic leadership as a strategic lever for women’s advancement: insights from the Indian automobile industry

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The healthcare sector faces leadership challenges, emphasizing the importance of a mechanism to support and empower team members. The present study aims to investigate the impact of team empowerment (TE) on team performance (TP), with the mediating role of shared leadership (SL) and the moderating role of relationship conflict between shared leadership and team performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study's conceptual model was proposed using the social exchange theory and conservation of resource theory. Data was collected using a self-administrated questionnaire to 492 respondents, of which 42 were team leaders, and 450 were team members from 42 teams in the Pakistani healthcare sector. The Partial Least Square-Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) technique was used to examine the proposed hypotheses of the study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results revealed a significant positive relationship between team empowerment and shared leadership. SL is positively associated with team performance. The present study also found that SL positively mediated the relationship between shared leadership and team performance. Moreover, relationship conflict moderated the relationship between SL and TP.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The finding delineates that healthcare organizations can adopt shared leadership and empower team members by involving them in decision-making, enhancing collaboration, resource utilization, and patient care outcomes. Managers should implement structured strategies like cross-functional training and inclusive decision-making processes to cultivate empowered teams and mitigate relationship conflicts for optimal performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study advocates developing shared leadership practices for better team outcomes. This study is an early attempt to examine the mediating role of shared leadership between team empowerment and team performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Unlocking team performance: the interplay of team empowerment, shared leadership, and relationship conflict in healthcare sector

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In manufacturing organizations, transformational leadership is not only about supervising tasks but also about shaping employees’ experiences of meaning, awareness, connection, support, and voluntary contribution. Drawing primarily on social exchange theory (SET) and transformational leadership perspectives, this study examines the association of perceived transformational leadership (PTL) with workplace spirituality dimensions, namely meaningful work, mindfulness, transcendence, compassion, and sense of community, along with its association with organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) among managerial employees in Indian manufacturing firms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study adopted a quantitative, cross-sectional research design. Data were collected from 412 managerial employees working in manufacturing firms in Chhattisgarh, India. The measurement and structural models were assessed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicate that PTL is positively and significantly associated with all five workplace spirituality dimensions and OCB. Among the workplace spirituality dimensions, sense of community showed the strongest association with PTL, followed by mindfulness, transcendence, compassion, and meaningful work. PTL also demonstrated a strong positive association with OCB, suggesting that supportive, inspirational, and individualized leadership behaviors may correspond with employees’ cooperative, discretionary, and extra-role behaviors. However, the relatively high associations involving transcendence indicate that its distinctiveness should be interpreted cautiously.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to workplace spirituality, transformational leadership, and OCB literature by positioning PTL as an important relational and organizational condition associated with employees’ spiritual work experiences and citizenship behavior. It offers context-specific empirical evidence from managerial employees in Indian manufacturing firms, an area that remains relatively underexplored in emerging economy research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Perceived transformational leadership, workplace spirituality and Organizational citizenship behavior: evidence from Indian manufacturing firms

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to investigate the impact of visionary leadership on employees’ psychological well-being, with job autonomy as a mediator and perceived organizational support (POS) as a moderator through the lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The research employs a time-lagged survey method, collecting data from 360 employees across public, private, and nongovernmental organizations in the UAE. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS4 software.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings support the positive impact of visionary leadership on employee psychological well-being. Job autonomy was confirmed as a significant mediator, and POS strengthened the relationship between visionary leadership and employee psychological well-being by enhancing the effects of job autonomy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among the practical implications, investment on developing visionary leadership is critical not only for the organizations but also for the well-being of employees. Furthermore, trusting and empowering workforce to take initiatives on their own (job autonomy) is also an important aspect that leadership must consider. Finally, a conducive organizational support must be in place to ensure that the well-being of employees is taken care of.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to leadership and well-being research by (a) positioning visionary leadership as a distinct antecedent of both hedonic and eudaimonic well-being; (b) integrating Self-Determination Theory to explain the motivational pathway via job autonomy; and (c) demonstrating the boundary-strengthening role of perceived organizational support in the UAE’s culturally collectivist context.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Impact of visionary leadership on employee’s psychological wellbeing: mediating role of job autonomy and moderating role of perceived organizational support

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping organizational processes and competitive dynamics across industries. Although scholarly interest in AI adoption is increasing, there remains a lack of research on how ethical leadership and technological sustainability affect organizational outcomes related to generative AI. This study investigates the role of virtue ethics in guiding the implementation of generative AI in HR-driven customer service contexts and examines how leadership perspectives influence the responsible and sustainable adoption of technology.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study draws on normative ethical theory and dynamic capability theory to develop a conceptual framework explaining how ethical leadership and organizational capabilities influence perceptions of generative AI performance. The research analyzes the mechanisms by which virtue-based ethical considerations and leadership-driven governance practices support the effective and responsible deployment of generative AI technologies. Data were collected from 335 respondents, and analysis was conducted using structural equation modelling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study indicates that ethical leadership grounded in virtue ethics is essential for fostering responsible generative AI adoption by strengthening employee trust, enhancing internal reputation, and supporting sustainable technology integration. Additionally, dynamic organizational capabilities enable the alignment of ethical governance with technological implementation, thereby improving perceived generative AI performance in HR-supported customer service environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research advances the literature on generative AI adoption by integrating virtue ethics and dynamic capability perspectives to explain how ethical governance and leadership influence AI-enabled organizational outcomes. The study underscores the significance of strategic leadership, ethical oversight, and sustainable technology management in maximizing the value that generative AI generates within organizational contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The behavioral ethical lens of generative AI application in organizations: from corporate reputation, leadership, and technological sustainability perspectives

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Given the growing recognition that family businesses play a significant role in the global economy, many studies have investigated leadership transitions, succession planning, and generational conflict. However, little is known about the challenges faced by nonfamily managers in family businesses. Therefore, this article aims to identify the barriers to leadership for nonfamily managers in large family-owned businesses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Authors studied a family business based in Brazil and collected data from 20 nonfamily leaders within the organization. Authors applied the fuzzy Delphi method and the fuzzy Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) method, as it is a decision-making support tool commonly used to address complex problems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>After applying an innovative methodological approach, authors identified eight barriers to leadership in large family businesses: recruitment, financial management, turnover, team development, client prospecting, training adaptation, transportation, and leadership development. Overcoming these obstacles requires strategic solutions such as the implementation of career development plans, standardized management models, leadership development programs, and increased family involvement to ensure long-term stability and business success.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings of this study provide actionable insights for managers in large family businesses, offering practical solutions to address common leadership barriers. Fostering greater family involvement in leadership processes may help reduce turnover and strengthen the company's long-term strategic direction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This article provides fresh insights into the challenges faced by nonfamily leaders in family businesses and explores how they can adjust their strategies to effectively overcome these key obstacles. Additionally, the research provides a comprehensive framework with solutions to these barriers, which may be valuable for managers of other large family businesses in emerging countries, in addition to enriching Agency Theory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Is blood thicker than water? Identifying barriers to leadership in family businesses

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study, uniquely employing a bibliometric approach, aims to fill this gap by identifying the intellectual foundations and key publications shaping DL research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A bibliometric analysis using Reference Publication Year Spectroscopy (RPYS) was conducted on 485 DL-related publications indexed in Web of Science. CRExplorer software processed citation data, clustered reference variations, and analyzed citation patterns.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seventeen highly cited references were identified as pivotal to DL’s conceptualization. Early research on transformational leadership, adaptive structuration theory, and virtual teams laid the foundation for DL. Recent studies emphasize its impact on innovation, performance, and employee well-being. The findings reveal a significant shift from microlevel leader–follower interactions to broader strategic perspectives, providing enlightening insights for the audience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study focuses on Web of Science-indexed publications, potentially excluding relevant contributions from other databases. Future research should explore DL’s practical applications across industries.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Understanding DL’s intellectual foundations is not just informative, but it also empowers leaders to develop competencies for digital transformation, informing leadership training and policy frameworks. This practical application of the research makes the audience feel capable and ready to face the challenges of digital transformation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>DL, by fostering inclusive organizations, enhancing digital literacy, and ensuring ethical and socially responsible digital transformation, can bring about positive social changes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This is the first systematic RPYS-based study on DL’s intellectual roots, offering valuable insights for researchers and practitioners.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Tracing the evolution of digital leadership: a bibliometric study employing reference publication year spectroscopy

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our study integrates three resource-related theories—social exchange, social learning, and self-verification—to investigate how laissez-faire leadership influences subordinates’ organizational citizenship behavior toward individuals (OCB-I). Hence, we introduce a comprehensive job demands-resources (JD-R) model, which positions laissez-faire leadership as a challenging job demand. This leadership style, characterized by a hands-off approach that encourages subordinates to seek resources, is examined concerning three key mechanisms-perceived organizational support (POS), coworker support, and learning goal orientation (LGO)-that mediate the relationship between laissez-faire leadership and subordinate OCB-I.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a cross-sectional survey design and an online questionnaire, we collected usable data from 203 Taiwanese employees in various industries and performed an Mplus analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our results show that (1) perceived organizational support and coworker support fully mediated the relationship between laissez-faire leadership and subordinate OCBI, (2) learning-goal orientation partially mediated the relationship, and (3) when multiple resources were simultaneously available in the workplace, coworker support outweighed other resources and benefited employees the most in the context of laissez-faire leadership.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research underscores the often overlooked but critically challenging job demand of laissez-faire leadership. By establishing a concurrent test of three functions of resources, our work sheds new light on how laissez-faire leadership can be effectively managed to enhance OCB-I. Our research also reveals how employees can overcome challenges by focusing on appropriate resources and fostering a willingness to assist colleagues through OCB-I. These practical implications empower leaders and practitioners to effectively manage laissez-faire leadership and enhance organizational citizenship behavior.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Laissez-faire leadership as a challenging job demand: looking at three theoretical perspectives on the mediating effects of resources

<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>In the modern virtual workplace, an organization's ability to complete projects successfully is essential to its future sustainability. Identifying the factors that contribute to successful project outcomes is crucial in project management research. This study seeks to examine how shared leadership affects the quality of teamwork and the success of information system development projects. It also explores how project complexity affects the success of information system development (ISD) projects in the context of virtual project teams, which are usually made up of knowledge workers with a lot of experience.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>Data collected from 509 virtual ISD project team members in Pakistan were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) with bootstrapping to assess the effects of shared leadership on teamwork quality and project success. The study also assessed the mediation role of teamwork and the moderation effect of project complexity on the mediation effect of teamwork quality between shared leadership and project success relationship.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>The study found a positive correlation between shared leadership, teamwork quality, and project success. This study also revealed that teamwork quality mediates the association between shared leadership and project success. Furthermore, the results demonstrated that teamwork quality and project complexity moderate-mediate the relationship between shared leadership and project success.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>Shared leadership enhances project success in virtual teams by improving teamwork. It requires investment in team development and collaboration initiatives, which ultimately lead to project success.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>The findings complement previous research with new insights on behavioral dimensions of shared leadership and their effects on outcomes on the level of the individual. To date, no prior study has employed this nascent methodology to investigate the relationship between shared leadership and project success.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Linking shared leadership and project success in virtual project teams: a moderated mediation model of teamwork and project complexity

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines the relationship between integrative leadership and strategic outcomes in complex adaptive systems. We aim to develop a theoretical framework that explains how leadership practices influence organizational adaptability in turbulent environments and provide practical guidance for organizational leaders.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We employed a multi-modal methodology combining systematic meta-analysis of 87 empirical studies (2010-2025) with multi-level network analysis of six multinational organizations. This approach enabled triangulation across different data sources and analytical techniques to comprehensively map leadership-strategy dynamics across diverse organizational contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We identified six mechanisms through which leadership and strategy co-evolve: collective sensemaking, adaptive tension management, network reconfiguration, paradoxical integration, distributed cognition, and temporal synchronization. Network analysis revealed three distinct leadership-strategy configurations, with distributed-integrated networks demonstrating superior adaptive capacity. Organizations with moderate centralization, high cross-level connectivity, and dense middle management clusters exhibited 37% higher adaptive performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our sample focused on large multinational organizations, potentially limiting generalizability to smaller entities or different cultural contexts. Future research should examine leadership-strategy dynamics in diverse organizational types, entrepreneurial ventures, and ecosystem contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For practitioners, we provide actionable guidance for developing leadership systems that enhance strategic adaptability, including recommendations for leadership development, organizational design, and strategic decision-making processes that enable simultaneous exploration and exploitation in complex environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By enhancing organizational adaptability, our framework contributes to organizational sustainability and resilience, potentially enabling more effective responses to societal challenges and promoting stable employment during periods of disruption and change.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study transcends traditional dichotomies between leadership and strategy by empirically mapping their co-evolution within complex adaptive systems, offering the novel concept of 34;network fluidity34; as a critical capability for strategic adaptation in volatile environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Integrative leadership in complex adaptive systems: a multi-modal analysis of strategic decision-making processes

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>With approximately 15–20% of people across the globe being Neurodivergent, leaders and academics must find ways to adapt communication to ensure inclusion. The aim of this research is to devise a framework for all to understand how to best communicate with each other that supports Neurodiversity inclusion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on over 300 online questionnaire responses, the authors explored the communication challenges faced by Neurodivergent individuals, specifically with non-Neuroinclusive leaders.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Neurodivergent people are conscious that they are “a-typical” and function, learn and process information differently from the majority who are Neurotypical. In many instances, the issue of what was said does not match what was heard, resulting in a response that is not the detail being sought. A change in language and approach is needed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Connecting the value of neurodiversity with communication strategies has the potential to support Neurodiversity inclusion as an organizational strength for increased business results. This can be applied in the development of support mechanisms for business school students as they develop their leadership skill set, or within an organization resulting in added competitive advantage.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This framework offers the ability to increase engagement by establishing a “way of working” between Neurodivergent and Neurotypical people, enabling the longevity and inclusion of Neurodiversity in the work environment. Thereby contributing to the Neurodiversity movement by offering an adaptable communication framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Unleashing the power of neurodiversity: giving voice in communication challenges for inclusive leadership – say what you mean and mean what you say

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on the knowledge- and resource-based view, this study seeks to determine how knowledge-oriented leadership contributes to Sustainable Performance across all dimensions of the triple bottom line, considering the mediating effects of the Sustainable Development Goals, knowledge workers’ social responsibility, and knowledge workers’ competence. In addition, it explores whether Green Intellectual Capital strengthens or weakens this relationship.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Survey data were collected from 413 employees in SMEs in China’s manufacturing and technology sectors; the proposed relationships were assessed through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study found that knowledge-oriented leadership does not directly influence sustainable performance; it affects sustainable performance only through mediating mechanisms. The findings further indicate that knowledge-oriented leadership significantly fosters alignment with the Sustainable Development Goals, as well as knowledge workers’ social responsibility and competence, ultimately enhancing Sustainable Performance. The analysis also revealed that Green intellectual capital positively moderates the knowledge-oriented leadership and sustainable performance relationship and strengthens the indirect pathway through SDGs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite its contributions, this study has several limitations. First, the data were collected from manufacturing and technology SMEs in China using a cross-sectional design, which limits the generalizability of the findings and does not allow causal relationships to be established. Future studies should employ longitudinal or multi-country designs to validate the proposed framework across different organizational and cultural contexts. Second, although this study identified SDG orientation, knowledge-worker social responsibility, and knowledge-worker competence as important mediating mechanisms, other organizational factors such as digital transformation, organizational learning, and innovation capability may also influence the relationship between knowledge-oriented leadership and sustainable performance. Finally, future research could further examine the role of green intellectual capital by exploring additional boundary conditions or conducting industry-specific analyses to determine whether its moderating influence varies across different organizational settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study’s relevance stems from the scarcity of research that offers a holistic understanding of how knowledge-oriented leadership contributes to sustainable performance and the mechanisms that translate KOL into sustainable performance outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: From knowledge-oriented leadership to triple-bottom-line outcomes: the mediating role of sustainable development goals, knowledge-worker responsibility, and competence

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates how the strategic alignment of Green Transformational Leadership (GTL), Green Human Resource Management (GHRM), and Green Organizational Culture (GOC) impacts Employee Green Behavior (EGB), with Green Self-Efficacy (GSE) serving as a mediating factor.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on the Stimulus-Organism-Response (SOR) framework, data were collected from 216 managerial employees of an Indonesian fertilizer company and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GHRM and GOC significantly enhanced GSE and indirectly fostered EGB. However, GTL had no significant direct or indirect effect on GSE or EGB. This highlights a novel insight: leadership, without reinforcement from HR systems and culture, may not be sufficient to influence sustainable employee behaviors. The study underscores that GSE is a critical psychological pathway through which aligned systems promote green behavior.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation, and findings are based on a single industrial sector in a developing economy. Broader industry and cross-cultural studies are encouraged.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Organizations should prioritize aligning HRM practices and culture with sustainability objectives and invest in building employee self-efficacy to maximize the effectiveness of green leadership. Policy initiatives could support this alignment through environmental literacy programs and performance-linked incentives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research uniquely applies the SOR model to explore strategic alignment in organizational sustainability and uncovers the conditional impact of leadership effectiveness in green behavior transformation, an area previously underexplored.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Strategic enablers of employee green behavior: the role of HRM, culture, and leadership alignment

strategy_and_leadership.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although there is broad agreement on the technological antecedents that improve technology adoption, most studies viewed technology-led human resource management as a single episode, ignoring that acceptance is only a part of the diffusion process. The study explored how the technological consequences of algorithmic human resource management (relative advantage, compatibility and complexity), the individual (i.e., user knowledge and attitude) and organizational factors (digital leadership) facilitate its adoption and continuous usage among human resource management professionals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study employed a quantitative design with empirical data from 165 senior human resource managers working in Ghana’s banking, insurance, media and telecommunication industries.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Results from the structural equation modelling revealed that, besides the technical aspects of algorithmic human resource management (i.e., relative advantage and compatibility), user knowledge, attitude and digital leadership become exceedingly central in easing its adoption and ensuring its continued use among non-ride-hailing firms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings have significant implications for organizational heads and human resource managers who seek to ensure the smooth transition of algorithmic human resource management into their human resource functions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The role of digital leadership: algorithmic human resource adoption and its continued use among human resource managers

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite increasing scholarly attention to digital transformation, limited research has examined how digital leadership translates into organizational performance through employee behavioral mechanisms and organizational capabilities. Addressing this gap, the present study investigates the direct and indirect effects of digital leadership on organizational performance through innovative work behavior and examines the moderating role of digital transformation capability in Industry 4.0 manufacturing organizations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A time-lagged survey design was employed to collect data from 400 employees working in manufacturing organizations located in Gujarat and Pune, India. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structure Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) to test the proposed relationships, mediation, and moderation effects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings reveal that digital leadership positively influences both innovative work behavior and organizational performance. Innovative work behavior significantly enhances organizational performance and partially mediates the relationship between digital leadership and organizational performance. Furthermore, digital transformation capability strengthens the positive effect of digital leadership on organizational performance. However, the moderated mediation effect was not supported.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study advances the digital leadership literature by integrating Social Exchange Theory and Dynamic Capabilities Theory within a multilevel framework. It contributes to existing knowledge by identifying innovative work behavior as a key behavioral mechanism and digital transformation capability as an important contextual enabler through which digital leadership enhances organizational performance in Industry 4.0 manufacturing environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Digital leadership and organizational performance in industry 4.0: a conditional process model of digital transformation capability and innovative work behavior

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Covid-19 pandemic accelerated the shift toward virtualized work, offering new opportunities for autonomy and flexibility while introducing unique challenges. Building on prior research linking transformational leadership and digital competence to positive outcomes in virtual teams, this study aims to examine how the temporal permanence of virtual work relates to employees’ perceptions of transformational leadership and digital competence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using survey data from 488 professionals across 18 industry clusters in Germany (June–August 2020), this study explores transformational leadership and digital competence during the pandemic. A cluster analysis identifies distinct temporal modes of virtual work based on the conditions before, during and after the pandemic. An analysis of variance examined how these modes affected the perception of transformational leadership and digital competence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study identifies three distinct modes of temporal permanence in virtual work environments following the pandemic’s onset. It further reveals that employees’ perceptions of transformational leadership and digital competence vary significantly depending on the temporal dimension of work virtualization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings suggest that organizations should integrate current or planned forms of virtual work into their development strategies, considering tailored interventions for different virtualization modes. Practical approaches for applying these insights in crisis and noncrisis contexts are discussed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research extends existing studies on virtual leadership and competence development by incorporating the temporal dimension of virtual work design. It recontextualizes known mechanisms and raises new questions about the dynamics of virtualized work.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Perception of transformational leadership and digital competence with varying degrees of permanence of virtual work: insights on work virtualization during the COVID-19 lockdown
